Questions marked "new": true are the newest additions: 15 each for chapters 27, 29, 30 and 32 (addedBatch 3) and 4 each for chapters 16, 19 and 31 (addedBatch 4). optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: A client had a laceration on the left forearm closed with sutures 6 hours ago. The wound edges are warm, with redness 0.5 cm from the wound and slight swelling. The client rates the pain 4 of 10 and makes a full fist with the left hand. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. The client's partner says, "Please do something before this turns into an infection." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document the findings and report them to the provider now as an early wound infection
options.rationale: Documenting is right, but the label is wrong. Warmth, redness, swelling, and pain 6 hours after closure do not establish infection.

options.text: Recheck the left forearm on a schedule and hold the documentation until a change appears
options.rationale: Rechecking is right, but the first set of findings is the baseline. Without it there is nothing to compare a change against.

options.text: Document the redness size, pain rating, and hand function with the time, then recheck on a schedule
options.rationale: These are the expected early findings of inflammation. Measured findings with a time give the baseline that later checks are compared with.

options.text: Document the findings and tell the partner that redness this soon means healing has been delayed
options.rationale: Redness this soon is expected. Vessels dilate and blood flow increases in the vascular response.

questions.takeaway: Early warmth, redness, swelling, and pain at a wound are expected. Record measured findings with the time so that later findings can be compared with baseline.
questions.strategy: Every option documents or rechecks, so read the second half of each one. Only one sets a measured baseline without adding a wrong label or a wrong delay.

steps.detail: Four cardinal signs, 6 hours after closure, function intact.
"As infection," "hold the documentation," and "healing delayed" are each one thing off.
Measured findings with a time, then a scheduled recheck.

elimination.verdict: Document measured findings with the time and recheck on a schedule.

questions.nursesNote:
Yesterday 0800, day 1 after closure of a left forearm laceration: wound edges warm, redness 0.5 cm from wound edge, swelling limited to the wound edges, pain 4 of 10, makes a full fist with left hand, oral temperature 36.7 °C.

Today 0800: Wound edges are warm. Redness is 0.3 cm from wound edge. Swelling extends to the left wrist. Pain is 4 of 10. Unable to make a full fist with left hand. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up.

segments.text: Wound edges are warm
segments.rationale: Warmth is a cardinal sign and matches yesterday's entry.

segments.text: Redness is 0.3 cm from wound edge
segments.rationale: Redness was 0.5 cm yesterday. It is smaller, which is not a worsening finding.

segments.text: Swelling extends to the left wrist
segments.rationale: Yesterday the swelling was limited to the wound edges. It has spread, and a worsening sign is followed up.

segments.text: Pain is 4 of 10
segments.rationale: Pain is a cardinal sign and the rating is unchanged from yesterday.

segments.text: Unable to make a full fist with left hand
segments.rationale: Yesterday the client made a full fist. Decreased function is a cardinal sign, and a loss from baseline is followed up.

segments.text: Oral temperature is 36.8 °C
segments.rationale: This reading is close to yesterday's 36.7 °C and does not change the plan. The local findings are judged against their own baseline.

questions.takeaway: A cardinal sign that matches baseline is expected. A cardinal sign that is worse than baseline is followed up, and function counts as much as redness.
questions.strategy: Do not highlight a finding because it is a sign of inflammation. Line up each of today's findings with yesterday's entry and highlight only what is worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Six findings in each entry.

steps.action: Mark what changed for the worse
steps.detail: Swelling has spread and the fist is lost.

steps.action: Leave what matches or is better
steps.detail: Warmth, pain, and temperature match. Redness is smaller.

questions.stem: A client had a laceration on the left forearm closed with sutures 3 days ago. Yesterday at 0800 the nurse marked the edge of the redness at 0.3 cm from the wound. The client rated pain 4 of 10, swelling reached the left wrist, and the client was unable to make a full fist. Today at 0800 the redness is 1 cm from the wound, past the marked line, and pain is 5 of 10. Swelling is back to the wound edges and the client makes a full fist. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the wider redness and higher pain now, and include that swelling and hand function are better
options.rationale: Redness has crossed the marked line and pain has risen. Worsening findings are reported, and the report gives the whole picture, including what is better.

options.text: Document all four changes and recheck at 2000, because swelling and hand function are better
options.rationale: Two findings are better, but two are worse. Improvement in one sign does not cancel worsening in another.

options.text: Report the wider redness and higher pain now as a wound infection that needs treatment
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but the label goes beyond the findings. Redness and pain alone do not establish infection.

options.text: Redraw the line at 1 cm and use today's redness and pain as the baseline from now on
options.rationale: A new mark helps later checks, but resetting the baseline without reporting hides the change just found.

questions.takeaway: Compare every sign with baseline. Worsening in any sign is reported, even when other signs are better, and the report states findings without naming a cause.
questions.strategy: The trend is mixed, which makes waiting look reasonable. The deciding cue is that redness has passed the marked line and pain is up: two signs moved the wrong way. Then choose the report that does not add a diagnosis.

steps.detail: Redness and pain are worse. Swelling and function are better.
Worsening symptoms are reported. Better signs do not cancel them.
One states findings. One adds "infection," which the findings do not establish.
Moving the baseline hides the change.

elimination.verdict: Report the wider redness and higher pain, with the improved swelling and function.

questions.stem: A client had a deep laceration of the left forearm that extended into the muscle. It was sutured 3 weeks ago and has healed with a firm scar. The client says, "The scar feels tight and my left grip is weaker than my right. Did the healing fail?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It did not fail. Once the scar matures, the muscle under it will work as it did before."
options.rationale: The first sentence is right. The promise is not: scar tissue does not work like the tissue it replaced.

options.text: "The scar shows that the repair stage did not finish, so the weak grip should be reported."
options.rationale: Scar formation is part of tissue repair. It does not show that the stage was left unfinished.

options.text: "It did not fail. A scar means that new muscle cells have replaced the damaged ones."
options.rationale: Replacement with new cells is regeneration. A scar is the other way tissue repairs.

options.text: "It did not fail. Scar is one way tissue repairs, and it may not work like the tissue it replaced."
options.rationale: Tissue repair happens by regeneration, scar formation, or both. The area returns toward normal function, and scar tissue does not function like the original tissue.

questions.takeaway: Tissue repair is regeneration, scar formation, or both. The area returns toward normal function, and scar does not work like the tissue it replaced.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options reassure the client that healing did not fail. Compare what each one says about the scar: full return, new muscle cells, or a repair that may not work like the original.

steps.action: Drop the option that calls repair unfinished
steps.detail: A scar is repair.
One promises full return and one describes regeneration.
"May not work like the tissue it replaced."

elimination.verdict: It did not fail, and scar may not work like the tissue it replaced.

questions.stem: A client recovered from a common cold 1 month ago. The client says, "Now that I have had a cold, I should not catch any colds this year." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your body made its own immunity, and the memory it formed will also protect you against most other cold viruses this season."
options.rationale: Making its own response and forming memory are right, but natural active immunity is specific to the virus that caused the illness.

options.text: "Your body made its own immunity to that one virus. A cold from a different virus can still make you sick."
options.rationale: Recovering from a cold gives natural active immunity to that specific virus. Adaptive responses target specific antigens, so other viruses are not covered.

options.text: "Your immunity came from antibodies from another source, so it will fade within the next few weeks."
options.rationale: Antibodies from another source describe passive immunity. After a natural infection, the client made the response.

options.text: "Your body made its own immunity to that one virus, but it will fade within a few weeks, like antibodies given to you from another source."
options.rationale: The scope is right, but the duration is not. Natural active immunity creates memory and provides long lasting protection; fading within weeks is a feature of passive immunity.

questions.takeaway: Recovering from an infection gives natural active immunity: the person makes the response, it creates memory, and it lasts, but it is specific to the organism that caused the infection.
questions.strategy: Two options limit the protection to that one virus, and two say the client made the immunity. Decide on duration, then on scope.

steps.detail: Recovery from a natural infection: natural active immunity.
The client made the response; no antibodies came from another source.
Active immunity creates memory and lasts, so the option that fades in weeks drops out.
Adaptive immunity is specific, so protection against other cold viruses drops out.

elimination.verdict: Immunity to that one virus; a different cold virus can still cause illness.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: At a wellness visit, a 78 year old client with no wounds says, "I had all my tetanus shots as a child more than 60 years ago, and vaccines create memory, so I am protected for life." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Those shots created memory cells, so if you ever get a deep wound, they will respond fast enough that you need no further dose."
options.rationale: Vaccines do create memory, but vaccine immunity needs booster doses to stay in place, and in older adults antibody duration is reduced further. Memory from 60 years ago cannot be counted on.

options.text: "Your protection has likely faded, so an injection of tetanus antibodies today will protect you for many years."
options.rationale: Fading protection is the right concern, but antibodies from another source give passive immunity: immediate, temporary, and with no memory. The client has no wound, so the goal is lasting protection.

options.text: "Your protection has likely faded, so a tetanus booster today will prompt your body to make its own antibodies again."
options.rationale: Vaccine immunity needs boosters, and at 78 antibody duration is reduced. A booster gives active immunity: the client makes the response again and memory is renewed, which suits a client seeking lasting protection.

options.text: "Your protection has faded because childhood shots give antibodies from another source, which the body clears over time."
options.rationale: Childhood vaccines give artificial active immunity: the client made the response. Antibodies from another source describe passive immunity.

questions.takeaway: Vaccination gives artificial active immunity with memory, and it needs boosters to stay in place; older adults have reduced antibody duration. When the goal is lasting protection rather than immediate cover, the client's own response is renewed with a booster, not with passive antibodies.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: B and C both restore protection. The deciding cue is that the client has no wound: the goal is lasting protection, and antibodies from another source give only immediate, short term protection with no memory.

steps.detail: Childhood tetanus shots: vaccination, artificial active immunity.
Vaccine immunity needs boosters, and at 78 antibody duration is shorter still.
Memory from 60 years ago cannot be counted on without a booster.
Antibodies from another source fade and leave no memory, and there is no wound calling for immediate cover.
Childhood shots made the client's own response.

elimination.verdict: A tetanus booster so the client makes antibodies again.

questions.stem: A client has never had a certain infectious disease and has never been vaccinated against it. The client was exposed to the disease this morning. Immune globulin is ordered. The client says, "I would rather have the vaccine today instead. I heard it lasts longer." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The vaccine does last longer, so it is the better choice for the exposure you had today."
options.rationale: Longer lasting is true, but active immunity takes time to develop, so it cannot be counted on alone for protection right now.

options.text: "Immune globulin protects you now but fades. A vaccine takes time but builds your own protection."
options.rationale: Passive immunity is immediate and temporary. Active immunity takes time, creates memory, and often lasts longer. Both halves are true and they explain the order.

options.text: "Immune globulin protects you now, and it also teaches your body to remember this disease."
options.rationale: The first half is right. The second is not: passive immunity does not create personal immune memory.

options.text: "The vaccine protects you now, and immune globulin is added later to make that protection last."
options.rationale: This reverses the two. The vaccine takes time, and immune globulin is the one that acts immediately.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity is immediate but temporary with no personal memory. Active immunity takes time to develop, creates memory, and often lasts longer.
questions.strategy: The client is right that a vaccine lasts longer, which makes the first option tempting. The stem's cue is timing: the exposure was this morning.

steps.detail: Exposed this morning, no immunity.

steps.action: Test each half of each option
steps.detail: Two options pair a true half with a false half, and one reverses both.

steps.action: Keep the option with two true halves
steps.detail: Now but fades, versus slow but the client's own.

elimination.verdict: Immune globulin protects now but fades. A vaccine takes time but builds the client's own protection.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client with no prior immunity to a disease was exposed to it and received immune globulin 1 hour ago. The client asks, "What kind of protection did that shot give me, and is it enough?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "This is artificial active immunity. It protects you now, and a vaccine when the provider advises gives longer protection."
options.rationale: Artificial active immunity follows vaccination, when the body makes its own response and the response takes time to develop. Immune globulin supplies antibodies made by another source, so the type is wrong.

options.text: "This is artificial passive immunity. It protects you now and keeps protecting you, so a vaccine is not needed."
options.rationale: The type is right, but passive protection is temporary and creates no personal immune memory. Immune globulin does not remove the need for the client's own response.

options.text: "This is natural passive immunity. It protects you now and keeps protecting you, so a vaccine is not needed."
options.rationale: This has two errors. Natural passive immunity is maternal antibodies passed through the placenta or breast milk, and immune globulin is a health care product, so it is artificial. Passive protection is also temporary, so the client still needs a vaccine for lasting protection.

options.text: "This is artificial passive immunity. It protects you now, and a vaccine when the provider advises gives longer protection."
options.rationale: Antibodies from another source given as a product are artificial passive immunity: immediate but temporary, with no personal memory. A vaccine produces active immunity, which creates memory and often lasts longer.

questions.takeaway: Immune globulin gives artificial passive immunity: immediate, temporary, and without personal memory. Lasting protection needs active immunity, such as a vaccine.
questions.strategy: Each option has two claims: the type of immunity and whether a vaccine is still needed. Judge each claim on its own; a wrong option can miss one or both.

steps.detail: Another source made the antibodies and they were given as a product: artificial passive. This removes A (active) and C (natural).
Passive protection is immediate but temporary, so a vaccine is still needed. This removes B and also C.
D names the right type and the need for the client's own response.

elimination.verdict: D. Artificial passive immunity protects now but fades; a vaccine builds the client's own lasting protection.

questions.stem: A client received immune globulin after an exposure to a disease. During the teaching, the client, who is breastfeeding a 2 month old infant, asks whether breast milk gives the infant any immune protection in general. After teaching, which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "My baby gets my antibodies through my milk now, and that protection is temporary."
options.rationale: Maternal antibodies in breast milk give natural passive immunity: immediate but temporary.

options.text: "My baby gets my antibodies through my milk now and will keep making them afterward."
options.rationale: The first half is right. But receiving antibodies does not create the infant's own immune memory.

options.text: "My baby got antibodies before birth through the placenta, so my milk adds nothing now."
options.rationale: Antibodies do cross the placenta, but breast milk is a second route of natural passive immunity.

options.text: "My baby will get my antibodies through my milk in a few weeks, once enough has built up."
options.rationale: A delay belongs to active immunity. Passive protection is immediate.

questions.takeaway: Maternal antibodies through the placenta or breast milk give natural passive immunity: immediate, temporary, and without personal memory.
questions.strategy: Every option contains something true about maternal antibodies. Check the second half of each for timing and for who is making the antibodies.

steps.detail: The breastfeeding client, not the infant.
Passive protection is immediate, not delayed.
Temporary, with no memory formed by the infant.

elimination.verdict: Antibodies through milk now, and the protection is temporary.

questions.stem: A client with no prior immunity to a disease received immune globulin after an exposure 3 months ago. The client received the first dose of the vaccine against the same disease 2 days ago. Today the client reports a new close exposure to the disease this morning and says, "I have had both, so I am covered." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "The immune globulin from 3 months ago is still working, so nothing more is needed today."
options.rationale: Passive protection is temporary. The nurse cannot assume it is still present 3 months later.

options.text: "The vaccine from 2 days ago covers you, because vaccines create immune memory."
options.rationale: Vaccines do create memory, but active immunity takes time to develop. Two days is too soon to count on it.

options.text: "Neither can be counted on today. One is temporary and the other needs time. I will report this exposure."
options.rationale: Passive protection fades and active protection has not had time to form. The client may be unprotected, so the nurse reports the exposure for a decision about protection now.

options.text: "Neither can be counted on today, so I will give you another dose of immune globulin now."
options.rationale: The reasoning is right and the product may be what is needed, but the nurse does not give it without an order. The exposure is reported first.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity is temporary and active immunity takes time to develop. A client can sit in the gap between the two.
questions.strategy: Each product sounds like it should cover the client, and two options lean on one of them. The deciding cues are the two time points: 3 months since the temporary product and 2 days since the slow one.

steps.detail: Immune globulin: immediate but temporary. Vaccine: lasting but slow.
3 months is long for a temporary product, and 2 days is too early for the other.
One acts without an order. One reports so that a decision can be made.

elimination.verdict: Neither can be counted on today, so the exposure is reported.

questions.stem: A client twisted the right ankle 1 hour ago and has never injured it before. The right ankle is already warm and swollen. The client asks, "How can my body react this fast to something it has never dealt with?" Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "This is your body's built in response. It starts right away because cells matched to this injury were ready."
options.rationale: Built in and immediate are right. The reason is not: cells matched to one specific target belong to adaptive immunity.

options.text: "This is your body's built in response. It starts right away and needs no earlier exposure."
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity: present at birth, rapid, broad, and ready without prior exposure.

options.text: "This is a targeted response. It starts right away because antibodies are already present."
options.rationale: A targeted response with antibodies describes adaptive immunity, which develops through exposure to antigens.

options.text: "This is your body's built in response. It will be faster next time because it creates memory."
options.rationale: Creating memory for a faster response next time is a feature of adaptive immunity, not of inflammation.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation is part of innate immunity: present at birth, rapid, broad, and needing no prior exposure. Memory and targeting belong to adaptive immunity.
questions.strategy: Three options begin the same way. The difference is the reason each gives, and only one reason belongs to the innate system.

steps.detail: One hour, first injury, already warm and swollen.
Matched cells, antibodies, and memory are all adaptive.
Needs no earlier exposure.

elimination.verdict: A built in response that needs no earlier exposure.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.scenario: A client twisted the right ankle 2 days ago. At 0800 today the nurse documented: right ankle warm, redness 4 cm across over the outer ankle, swelling limited to the ankle, pain 4 of 10, and able to bear weight with a limp. The nurse reassesses at 1600.
questions.stem: For each 1600 finding, indicate whether it is expected with inflammation or requires follow-up.

rows.text: Right ankle is warm to the touch
rows.rationale: Warmth is a cardinal sign and has not changed from the 0800 baseline.

rows.text: Swelling reaches the middle of the right calf
rows.rationale: Swelling has spread beyond the 0800 baseline. Worsening findings are reported.

rows.text: Pain is 4 of 10
rows.rationale: Pain is a cardinal sign and the rating is unchanged from 0800.

rows.text: Client cannot bear weight on the right leg
rows.rationale: Function has decreased since 0800, when the client could bear weight with a limp.

rows.text: Redness over the outer right ankle is 2 cm across
rows.rationale: The redness was 4 cm across at 0800, so it is smaller. A cardinal sign that is easing is not a worsening finding.

questions.takeaway: A cardinal sign that matches or is better than baseline is expected. A sign that has worsened since baseline needs follow-up.
questions.strategy: Do not judge each finding by whether it is a cardinal sign. Judge it against the 0800 entry: same, better, or worse?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0800: warm, redness 4 cm across, swelling at the ankle only, pain 4 of 10, bears weight with a limp.
Warmth and pain match, redness is less, swelling and function are worse.
Only worsening signs are reported.

elimination.verdict: Warmth, pain, and smaller redness are expected. Spreading swelling and lost weight bearing require follow-up.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A client fell onto an outstretched right hand 4 hours ago. Imaging shows no fracture. The client has deeply pigmented skin. The nurse assesses both wrists and compares the right with the left. Which findings does the nurse document as cardinal signs of inflammation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skin over the right wrist is warmer to the touch than the left wrist
options.rationale: Local warmth at the injured site, compared with the other wrist, is a cardinal sign of inflammation.

options.text: Skin over the right wrist is darker than skin over the left wrist
options.rationale: In deeply pigmented skin, the redness of inflammation can appear as a darker color. A color change at the site is the cardinal sign of redness.

options.text: Right wrist circumference is 2 cm larger than the left wrist
options.rationale: A larger circumference on the injured side is measured swelling, a cardinal sign.

options.text: Client is unable to turn a doorknob with the right hand
options.rationale: Decreased function is the fifth cardinal sign and the one most often left out. Losing a task the hand can normally do counts.

options.text: Oral temperature is 37.0 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C)
options.rationale: Warmth as a cardinal sign is local, felt at the site. A core temperature within the reference range is not one of the five signs.

options.text: Capillary refill in the right fingers is 2 seconds (reference under 3 seconds)
options.rationale: This checks circulation beyond the injury and is within the reference range. It is not one of the five cardinal signs.

questions.takeaway: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and decreased function, all found at the site. In deeply pigmented skin, redness can show as a darker color, and lost function counts as fully as swelling.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Recite the five signs and match each option to one of them. Warmth means warmth at the site, not core temperature, and a color change is the redness sign even when it does not look red.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warmth, redness, swelling, pain, decreased function.
Warmer right wrist, darker right wrist, larger right wrist, lost doorknob task.

steps.action: Reject the systemic and circulation checks
steps.detail: Oral temperature and capillary refill are not among the five, and both are within reference ranges.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.stem: A client touched a hot pan with the left palm 1 hour ago. The palm is warm, red, and swollen, and the skin is intact. The client asks what the body is doing to heal the burn. Place the events of the inflammatory response in the order in which they occur.

options.text: White blood cells move through the blood vessel walls into the burned area
options.rationale: This begins the cellular response, the second stage. Cells arrive after the vascular response has opened the way.

options.text: Blood vessels in the left palm dilate and blood flow to the area increases
options.rationale: Vessel dilation starts the vascular response, the first stage. Histamine released at the site causes this dilation, which produces the warmth and redness.

options.text: The area heals by new cells, scar, or both and returns toward normal function
options.rationale: Tissue repair is the third stage. Damaged tissue heals by regeneration, scar formation, or both.

options.text: Fluid moves out of the vessels into the tissue and the palm swells
options.rationale: Still in the vascular response: fluid leaves the dilated vessels, causing swelling and helping deliver immune cells.

options.text: Neutrophils and macrophages engulf dead cells and harmful material
options.rationale: Once in the area, white blood cells remove harmful material and dead cells by phagocytosis, completing the cellular response.

options.text: Mast cells and basophils in the left palm release histamine
options.rationale: Mast cells and basophils release histamine and other substances that promote inflammation. Histamine release comes first because it is what dilates the vessels in the vascular response.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation runs in three stages: vascular (histamine release, dilation, then fluid shift and swelling), cellular (white cells migrate in, then engulf), and tissue repair (regeneration, scar, or both).
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the six events into the three stages first, then order the two events inside each stage. Within a stage, something has to arrive before it can act.

steps.detail: Histamine release, dilation, and fluid shift are vascular. Migration and engulfing are cellular. Healing is repair.
Histamine release comes first; it is what dilates the vessels.
Vessels dilate before fluid can leave them.
White cells must move into the area before they can engulf anything.
The area returns toward normal function at the end.

elimination.verdict: Histamine release, dilation, fluid shift and swelling, white cell migration, engulfing, tissue repair.

questions.stem: A nurse at a clinic reviews the immunity history of six clients. Which clients have active immunity? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client who has measles antibodies 10 years after recovering from measles
options.rationale: The body made its own response to a natural infection. This is natural active immunity, which develops memory and long lasting protection.

options.text: A client who received an antitoxin in the emergency department after a venomous snakebite
options.rationale: An antitoxin supplies protection made by another source, given as a product. This is artificial passive immunity.

options.text: A 3 month old infant who receives antibodies in the parent's breast milk
options.rationale: The antibodies came from another source, the parent, by a natural route. This is natural passive immunity: immediate but temporary.

options.text: A client who received a vaccine containing a weakened virus
options.rationale: A vaccine introduces a weakened pathogen so the body produces its own response without causing the disease. This is artificial active immunity.

options.text: A client who received a vaccine containing an inactivated pathogen
options.rationale: Inactivated sounds like nothing happens, but the body still makes its own response to the vaccine. Vaccines give artificial active immunity.

options.text: A client who received immune globulin after an exposure to a disease
options.rationale: Immune globulin is antibodies made by another source and given as a product. This is artificial passive immunity, which creates no personal memory.

questions.takeaway: Ask who made the response. If the client made it, after an illness or a vaccine, it is active. If another source made it, as with breast milk, an antitoxin, or immune globulin, it is passive.
questions.strategy: Do not sort by how the product sounds. Ask one question of each client: did this person's own body make the response?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recovery from measles and both vaccines led the client's own body to respond: active.
Breast milk, an antitoxin, and immune globulin all bring antibodies from another source: passive.
An inactivated pathogen in a vaccine still triggers the client's own response, so it is active.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A client had a splinter removed from the right index finger 3 days ago. Within hours of the injury the fingertip became warm and swollen. Yesterday the client received a vaccine against a disease the client has never had. The client asks, "My finger reacted within hours. Why will the vaccine take longer to protect me?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your finger used an inborn, broad response. A vaccine response builds over time, targets one threat, and leaves memory."
options.rationale: Innate immunity is present at birth, rapid, and broad. Adaptive immunity develops through exposure to antigens, targets specific threats, and creates memory.

options.text: "Your finger reacted fast because it remembered your earlier splinters. The vaccine response is new to you, so it takes time."
options.rationale: The vaccine half is close, but memory belongs to adaptive immunity. The finger response needs no prior exposure.

options.text: "Your finger used a built in, broad response. The vaccine is slower because its antibodies come from another source."
options.rationale: The finger half is right. Antibodies from another source describe passive immunity, which acts immediately, not a vaccine.

options.text: "Your finger made a response aimed only at this one splinter. The vaccine response is slower because it is broad and general."
options.rationale: This reverses the two systems. The innate response is broad, and the adaptive response targets a specific antigen.

questions.takeaway: Innate immunity is present at birth, rapid, and broad, with no prior exposure needed. Adaptive immunity develops through exposure to antigens, targets one threat with B and T cells, and creates memory.
questions.strategy: Each option has two halves. Check the finger half for innate features and the vaccine half for adaptive features. One option gets both halves right.

steps.detail: Finger: inflammation, part of innate immunity. Vaccine: adaptive immunity.
Remembered and aimed at this splinter are adaptive features, so two options drop out.
Antibodies from another source is passive immunity, so that option drops out.

elimination.verdict: Innate is fast and broad. Adaptive develops over time, is specific, and leaves memory.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A nurse at a clinic reviews four client histories while preparing for possible measles exposures over the coming year. Which client is most likely to have a fast, specific immune response if exposed to measles 1 year from now?

options.text: A client who received immune globulin containing measles antibodies yesterday
options.rationale: This client has measles specific protection now, but passive protection is temporary and creates no personal memory, so it will not last a year.

options.text: A client whose skin becomes red and swollen within hours of every minor cut
options.rationale: A fast local reaction is inflammation, part of innate immunity. It is rapid but broad, not specific to measles, and creates no memory.

options.text: A client who received a measles vaccine 1 year ago and has had no measles exposure since then
options.rationale: Vaccination gives artificial active immunity. The client produced the response and has memory for measles, which supports a faster, stronger response on future exposure.

options.text: A 2 month old infant who received measles antibodies across the placenta from a parent who had measles as a child
options.rationale: Antibodies across the placenta give natural passive immunity: immediate but temporary, and the infant forms no memory of its own.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity protects at once but fades and leaves no memory. Inflammation is fast but broad. Only active immunity creates the memory that gives a fast, specific response on a later exposure.
questions.strategy: Two options give measles specific protection. The deciding cue is 1 year from now: immune globulin protects at once but is temporary and leaves no memory, so only the vaccinated client will make a fast, specific response then.

steps.action: Reject the fast but broad response
steps.detail: Inflammation is innate and not specific.
Antibodies from another source fade and leave no memory.
The vaccinated client made their own response and has memory cells.

elimination.verdict: The client vaccinated against measles 1 year ago.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A nurse reviews immune events described in six client records. Which events are part of innate immunity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Neutrophils engulf bacteria at a splinter wound in the right thumb within hours of the injury
options.rationale: Phagocytosis by neutrophils is part of innate immunity: rapid, broad, and ready without prior exposure. Engulfing bacteria sounds targeted, but the same response meets any harmful material.

options.text: Plasma cells release antibodies that bind one specific antigen 2 weeks after a vaccine
options.rationale: B lymphocytes become antibody producing plasma cells when activated by an antigen. This is antibody mediated (humoral) immunity, part of the adaptive system.

options.text: T lymphocytes target lung cells that are infected with a virus
options.rationale: Cell mediated immunity uses T lymphocytes to target infected or abnormal cells. It is part of the adaptive system.

options.text: Redness and swelling develop at a vaccine injection site in the left upper arm within 6 hours
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity, even when the trigger is a vaccine. The antibodies the vaccine is meant to produce come later, from the adaptive system.

options.text: A second exposure to a virus produces a faster, stronger response than the first exposure did
options.rationale: Memory cells that allow a faster, stronger response on a later exposure are the key feature of adaptive immunity. Innate responses do not build memory.

options.text: Macrophages remove dead cells and debris from a burn on the left palm within hours of the injury
options.rationale: Macrophages are phagocytes that remove microbes, debris, and dead cells. Phagocytosis is part of innate immunity.

questions.takeaway: Innate immunity is present at birth, rapid, and broad, and it includes inflammation and phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages. Adaptive immunity develops through exposure to antigens, uses B and T lymphocytes, targets specific threats, and creates memory.
questions.strategy: Sort by the response, not by the trigger. Inflammation and engulfing by phagocytes are innate, even at a vaccine site. Plasma cells, antibodies, T lymphocytes, and memory are adaptive.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the response in each option
steps.detail: Phagocytosis, antibodies, T lymphocytes, inflammation, memory, and removal of debris.
Neutrophils engulfing bacteria and macrophages removing dead cells are innate.
Plasma cells from B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes, and a faster second response are adaptive.
The word vaccine pulls toward adaptive, but redness and swelling within hours are inflammation.

elimination.verdict: A, D, F.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A client scraped the right knee on gravel 1 hour ago. The skin around the scrape is warm and red. The client asks, "What is my body doing to my knee right now and over the next few hours?" Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The warmth and redness come from wider vessels and more blood flow. Next, white cells enter the knee in the tissue repair stage, and basophils and macrophages engulf debris."
options.rationale: This has two errors. White blood cells migrating into the tissue is the cellular response; tissue repair follows it. Basophils release histamine and other substances that promote inflammation; they do not engulf material.

options.text: "The warmth and redness come from wider vessels and more blood flow. Next, white cells enter the knee in the cellular response, and neutrophils and macrophages engulf debris."
options.rationale: In the vascular response, vessels dilate and blood flow increases, producing warmth and redness. In the cellular response, white blood cells migrate through the vessel walls, and neutrophils and macrophages perform phagocytosis.

options.text: "The warmth and redness come from fluid leaving the vessels. Next, white cells enter the knee in the cellular response, and basophils and macrophages engulf debris."
options.rationale: This has two errors. Fluid leaving the vessels causes swelling; warmth and redness come from dilated vessels and increased blood flow. Basophils release histamine and do not engulf material.

options.text: "The warmth and redness come from fluid leaving the vessels. Next, white cells enter the knee in the tissue repair stage, and neutrophils and macrophages engulf debris."
options.rationale: This has two errors. Fluid leaving the vessels causes swelling, not warmth and redness. White blood cells migrating into the tissue is the cellular response; tissue repair, by regeneration, scar formation, or both, follows it.

questions.takeaway: Vascular response: vessels dilate (warmth, redness) and fluid shifts out (swelling). Cellular response: white blood cells migrate in, and neutrophils and macrophages engulf harmful material. Tissue repair follows.
questions.strategy: Each option makes three claims: the cause of warmth and redness, the name of the stage, and the engulfing cells. Test each claim on its own; only one option gets all three right.

steps.action: Check the cause of warmth and redness
steps.detail: More blood at the site explains warmth and redness. Fluid leaving the vessels explains swelling, which removes C and D.
White cells crossing into the tissue is the cellular response, which removes A.
Only neutrophils and macrophages are phagocytes. Basophils release histamine, which confirms A and C are wrong.

elimination.verdict: B. Dilated vessels and more blood flow cause warmth and redness; white cells entering the tissue is the cellular response; neutrophils and macrophages engulf the debris.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A client sprained the left ankle 2 hours ago. The skin is intact. Left ankle circumference is 3 cm larger than the right, and the client rates the pain 5 of 10. The client asks, "Why does my body make it swell like this? Isn't the swelling just more damage?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The swelling is damage from the injury itself. Your body starts its healing response once the swelling goes down."
options.rationale: Swelling is part of the body's response, not a separate injury, and the response does not wait for the swelling to resolve.

options.text: "Widened vessels let white blood cells crowd into the ankle tissue, and those cells are what make up the swelling."
options.rationale: White blood cells do migrate into the area in the cellular response, but the swelling comes from fluid moving out of the vessels.

options.text: "Widened vessels bring extra blood into the ankle, and the extra blood inside the vessels is what makes it swell."
options.rationale: Blood flow does increase, but that causes warmth and redness. The swelling is fluid that has moved out of the vessels into the tissue.

options.text: "Widened vessels let fluid move into the ankle tissue. The fluid causes the swelling and brings in immune cells."
options.rationale: In the vascular response, vessels dilate and fluid moves into the tissue, causing swelling and helping deliver immune cells to the injury.

questions.takeaway: In the vascular response, vessels dilate and fluid moves from the vessels into the tissue. The fluid causes swelling and helps deliver immune cells to the injury.
questions.strategy: Three options start with widened vessels. Ask what actually makes up the swelling: fluid in the tissue, blood in the vessels, or cells.

steps.detail: Two hours after a sprain, with swelling: the vascular response.
More blood flow explains warmth and redness, not swelling.
Swelling is part of the response, not a separate injury.

steps.action: Compare the remaining widened vessel options
steps.detail: Swelling is fluid in the tissue, not white blood cells.

elimination.verdict: Fluid from dilated vessels causes the swelling and helps bring immune cells in.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A client takes an immunosuppressant daily after a kidney transplant. The client has a 2 cm abrasion on the right shin from a fall 2 days ago. Findings: redness 0.2 cm from the wound edge, no swelling, pain 1 of 10, walks without a limp, oral temperature 36.9 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C). The client says, "It barely looks irritated, so I can stop the daily wound checks you taught me." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Your medication can hide signs of infection. Check the wound daily and report new or spreading redness, drainage, or pain, even without fever."
options.rationale: An immunosuppressant affects immune function, so the signs of inflammation and infection can be muted, and infection can be present without fever when immunity is decreased. Daily checks continue, and worsening local findings are reported.

options.text: "Keep checking the wound every day, and call the clinic if your temperature rises above 37.2 °C, since fever is the clearest sign of infection."
options.rationale: Daily checks are right, but this plan waits for fever. Infection can be present without fever, especially when immunity is decreased, as it is with this client's medication.

options.text: "These findings are mild and your temperature is in the reference range, so you can stop the checks once the redness fades."
options.rationale: For a client with a typical immune response, mild signs with a temperature in range are reassuring. This client's medication means mild signs cannot be taken at face value.

options.text: "Your medication lowers your immune response, so these mild findings mean an infection has already started in the wound."
options.rationale: The first half is right. Mild findings do not establish infection, and the nurse does not label a cause from these findings.

questions.takeaway: Medications that suppress immunity can blunt the cardinal signs, and infection can be present without fever when immunity is decreased. Teach daily checks and reporting of new or spreading local findings, not waiting for fever.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the daily checks. The deciding cue is the immunosuppressant: infection can be present without fever, so a plan that waits for fever can miss it.

steps.detail: Daily immunosuppressant after a transplant.
Mild findings are not reassuring when the immune response is muted.
Mild findings do not prove infection has started.

steps.action: Compare the two daily check plans
steps.detail: One waits for fever; the other reports local changes even without fever.

elimination.verdict: Check daily and report local changes even without fever.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A client has a splinter wound in the left index finger that was removed 4 hours ago. Bacteria entered the wound, and the cellular response is underway. White blood cells have crossed the vessel walls into the finger tissue, and a neutrophil has recognized the bacteria as harmful material. Which event occurs next?

options.text: The neutrophil ingests the bacteria it has identified
options.rationale: Ingesting is the core of phagocytosis, which makes it tempting. It comes after the cell has surrounded the material.

options.text: More white blood cells cross into the finger tissue
options.rationale: Migration into the tissue comes first in the cellular response, and the stem states that it has already happened. A cell must arrive before it can act.

options.text: The bacteria are broken down inside the neutrophil
options.rationale: Breakdown is the last step of phagocytosis. It removes microbes and damaged tissue, but only after the material has been ingested.

options.text: The neutrophil surrounds the bacteria it has identified
options.rationale: Phagocytosis follows a fixed order: recognize, surround, ingest, and break down. Once the cell has recognized the material as harmful, it surrounds it.

questions.takeaway: In the cellular response, white blood cells migrate into the tissue first. Phagocytosis then follows a fixed order: recognize, surround, ingest, and break down the material.
questions.strategy: Ingesting is the step everyone remembers, so it pulls first. Ask what each step needs before it can happen: a cell cannot take in material it has not first wrapped.

steps.detail: Migration and recognition are done. The question asks for the step that follows recognition.
Crossing into the tissue happens before recognition.
Ingesting needs the material surrounded first, and breakdown needs it ingested.
Surrounding follows recognition.

elimination.verdict: D. The neutrophil surrounds the bacteria; ingestion and breakdown follow.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A client recovering from a viral illness asks how the body fights a specific germ. The nurse explains adaptive immunity. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "B lymphocytes become plasma cells, and plasma cells make antibodies."
options.rationale: When activated by an antigen, B lymphocytes differentiate into antibody producing plasma cells. This is antibody mediated (humoral) immunity.

options.text: "Antibodies bind to one specific antigen and neutralize or remove it."
options.rationale: Antibodies, also called immunoglobulins, bind specific antigens and neutralize or remove foreign material.

options.text: "T lymphocytes make the antibodies that destroy infected body cells."
options.rationale: T lymphocytes do target infected cells, but they do not make antibodies. Antibodies come from plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes.

options.text: "T lymphocytes target infected or abnormal body cells and help coordinate the response."
options.rationale: Cell mediated immunity uses T lymphocytes to target infected or abnormal cells, and T lymphocytes help coordinate immune responses.

options.text: "If the same germ returns, memory cells make the response faster and stronger."
options.rationale: Adaptive immunity creates memory cells that enable faster, stronger responses on a future exposure.

options.text: "If the same germ returns, the response starts over, because the antibodies from the first illness are gone."
options.rationale: Even when antibody levels fall, memory cells remain. The second response is faster and stronger, not a fresh start.

questions.takeaway: Adaptive immunity uses B lymphocytes (plasma cells making antibodies that bind specific antigens) and T lymphocytes (targeting infected or abnormal cells and coordinating the response), and it creates memory for a faster, stronger second response.
questions.strategy: Check each statement for which cell does what, then apply memory. Only the B cell line makes antibodies, and a returning germ meets memory cells, not a blank slate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: B cells through plasma cells, not T cells.
Target infected or abnormal cells and coordinate the response.
A second exposure brings a faster, stronger response.
Memory cells remain even when antibodies from the first illness are gone.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E.

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for Patients With Infection

questions.stem: An 81 year old client is admitted for a wound on the left lower leg. The admission history shows a daily immunosuppressant and less than half of each meal eaten for the past 3 weeks. Oral temperature is 36.7 °C. Redness extends 1 cm around the wound. Which conclusion guides the nurse's plan of care?

options.text: All three history findings raise concern, so the wound is reported on admission as infected
options.rationale: The history does raise concern, but redness of 1 cm does not establish infection.

options.text: Age and the medication raise concern, while food intake matters for healing but not for immune protection
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function as well as healing. All three findings count.

options.text: All three history findings raise concern, but closer assessment begins only if a fever develops
options.rationale: The concern is right, but the trigger is wrong. The plan follows from the history now, without waiting for a fever.

options.text: All three history findings raise concern, so closer assessment against baseline is planned from admission
options.rationale: Advanced age, an immunosuppressant, and poor nutrition each affect immunity. Reviewing the history identifies them so the plan can start now.

questions.takeaway: Age, nutritional status, disease, medications, and environmental exposures affect immunity. The history tells you whose protection is weak, and the plan starts from there.
questions.strategy: Three options accept that all three findings matter. They differ in what the nurse does next: label the wound, wait for a fever, or assess more closely now.

steps.detail: Age 81, daily immunosuppressant, poor intake for 3 weeks.

steps.action: Drop the option that discounts one
steps.detail: Nutrition affects immune protection too.
Labeling infection overreaches, and waiting for fever delays.

elimination.verdict: All three raise concern, so closer assessment against baseline starts on admission.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: An 81 year old client is admitted with a wound on the left lower leg. The nurse reviews the history to identify factors that may affect the client's immune protection. Which information does the nurse review for this purpose? Select all that apply.

options.text: Current medications, including any that suppress the immune system
options.rationale: Immunosuppressants can affect immune function.

options.text: Recent food intake and any change in weight
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function. Protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing.

options.text: Chronic health conditions
options.rationale: Chronic disease impacts immune competence and disease susceptibility.

options.text: Pain rating at the wound today
options.rationale: This is an assessment finding to compare with baseline. It is not a factor that affects immune protection.

options.text: Recent environmental exposures
options.rationale: Environmental exposures are one of the factors that affect immunity.

options.text: Size of the redness around the wound on admission
options.rationale: This is the baseline for the wound. It is not a factor that affects immune protection.

questions.takeaway: The factors that affect immunity are age and developmental stage, nutritional status, disease and overall health, medications, and environmental exposures.
questions.strategy: Every option is something the nurse collects. Separate the factors that affect immune protection from the findings that describe the wound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age, nutrition, disease, medications, environmental exposures.
Medications, intake and weight, chronic conditions, and exposures all match.

steps.action: Leave out what does not match
steps.detail: A pain rating and the size of the redness are findings, not factors.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: An 81 year old client was admitted 2 days ago with a wound on the left lower leg. The client takes a daily immunosuppressant and has eaten about one quarter of each meal since admission. Today the redness extends 1 cm around the wound, the same as on admission. The area is warm with mild swelling, both as on admission. Pain is 2 of 10, the same as on admission, and the client walks to the bathroom as on admission. Oral temperature is 36.6 °C.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Compare the wound findings with the admission baseline at each assessment
options.rationale: The findings match baseline now. Comparing over time is how a change will be recognized in a client whose protection is reduced.

options.text: Arrange a review of the client's intake of protein, vitamins, and minerals
options.rationale: The client eats one quarter of each meal. Adequate protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing.

options.text: Report the wound to the provider today as infected
options.rationale: Redness of 1 cm that is unchanged from admission does not establish infection.

options.text: Hold further wound checks until the provider has reviewed the nutrition plan
options.rationale: Nutrition matters, but assessment of the wound continues. Three factors lower this client's immune protection.

options.text: Inflammation at the wound in a client with reduced immune protection
options.rationale: The local findings are unchanged cardinal signs, and age, an immunosuppressant, and poor intake each reduce immune protection.

options.text: Wound infection, shown by redness and warmth
options.rationale: Redness and warmth alone do not establish infection, and neither has changed.

options.text: Expected healing with no added risk
options.rationale: The local findings fit, but the history adds risk.

options.text: Failure of the tissue repair stage
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings shows that repair has failed at 2 days.

options.text: Size of the redness and swelling around the wound
options.rationale: Color change and swelling are assessed and compared with baseline.

options.text: Pain rating and ability to walk on the left leg
options.rationale: Pain and functional ability are assessed and compared with baseline.

options.text: Oral temperature as the only sign of change
options.rationale: Temperature is one finding. Changes in the site, in pain, and in function are compared with baseline as well.

options.text: Size of the redness alone, measured once a day
options.rationale: Redness is one of several findings, and this client's history calls for closer assessment, not less.

questions.takeaway: Unchanged cardinal signs point to inflammation. A history of advanced age, an immunosuppressant, and poor intake means the nurse keeps comparing with baseline and acts on nutrition.
questions.strategy: Settle the condition first. Unchanged local findings rule out calling it infection, and the history rules out calling it risk free. The actions and parameters then follow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unchanged cardinal signs plus three factors that reduce protection.
Keep comparing with baseline and act on the poor intake.
The findings the nurse assesses: color, swelling, pain, function.

elimination.verdict: Inflammation with reduced immune protection; compare with baseline and review nutrition; monitor redness and swelling, pain and walking.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: An 81 year old client was admitted 3 days ago with a wound on the left lower leg and takes a daily immunosuppressant. On admission the client was alert, talkative, and ate about one quarter of each meal. Today the redness is 1 cm around the wound and pain is 2 of 10, both the same as on admission. Oral temperature is 36.5 °C. The client has slept through two meals, is slow to answer questions, and ate a few bites at breakfast. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the change in alertness and intake now, even though the wound and temperature are unchanged
options.rationale: The client has changed from baseline in behavior and function. In a client with reduced immune protection, the nurse does not rely on the wound or on fever alone, and worsening is reported.

options.text: Wake the client for lunch, encourage fluids, and report if alertness is no better this afternoon
options.rationale: Supporting intake is reasonable care, but it delays the report of a change from baseline in a client with reduced immune protection.

options.text: Report the wound as infected now, because the client is at risk and is sleeping more than before
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but the wound findings have not changed. The report should state what changed, not name a cause.

options.text: Document the change in alertness, and report it if the temperature rises above the admission reading
options.rationale: This client takes an immunosuppressant and is 81 years old. The nurse does not wait for a fever before acting on a change in behavior.

questions.takeaway: Compare the whole client with baseline, not only the wound. A change in behavior or function is reported, and fever is not required, especially when immune protection is reduced.
questions.strategy: The wound and the temperature both say nothing has changed, which makes waiting look reasonable. The deciding cue is the client: alert and talkative on admission, now slow to answer and sleeping through meals.

steps.detail: Unchanged.
Alertness and intake are both worse than on admission.
Age 81 and an immunosuppressant: do not wait for fever.

steps.action: Choose the report that states findings
steps.detail: One report names infection, which the wound does not support.

elimination.verdict: Report the change in alertness and intake now.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the admission note for a client. Which findings increase the client's risk for infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day
options.rationale: Nicotine use is a host factor that raises infection risk.

options.text: Indwelling urinary catheter placed in the emergency department
options.rationale: Invasive devices bypass natural barriers, and genitourinary infections often develop from catheter use.

options.text: Healed surgical scar on the left knee from 2 years ago
options.rationale: The scar is closed, so the skin barrier is intact. Intact skin is the best barrier against infection.

options.text: Body mass index 36 kg/m2 (reference range 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2)
options.rationale: This value is above the reference range. Obesity is a host factor that raises infection risk.

options.text: Received influenza vaccine 1 month ago
options.rationale: Vaccination reduces risk for the infections the vaccine covers.

options.text: Oral temperature 36.8 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C)
options.rationale: This reading is inside the reference range and describes the present state, not a risk factor.

questions.takeaway: Infection risk rises when barriers are bypassed, as with a urinary catheter, and with host factors such as nicotine use and obesity. Intact skin, including a healed scar, and vaccination protect.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The urinary catheter is easy to read past because it is routine care. Ask of each finding whether it breaks a barrier, bypasses one, or weakens the host.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The indwelling urinary catheter gives pathogens a route past natural barriers.
Smoking, and obesity shown by a body mass index of 36 kg/m2.
A healed scar is intact skin, and the vaccine lowers risk.
A temperature inside the range describes now, not risk.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client with sepsis from an infected wound on the left lower leg has received the prescribed antimicrobial and intravenous fluids for 12 hours. The nurse compares findings at 0600 with the findings recorded when sepsis was suspected at 1800. Which findings at 0600 require further escalation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Alert and oriented, as on admission; at 1800 the client was confused
options.rationale: Mental status moving back toward baseline is a sign of response to treatment.

options.text: Urine output 45 mL/hr (reference range at least 30 mL/hr); at 1800 it was 15 mL/hr
options.rationale: Urine output is a key marker of perfusion, and it is now inside the range.

options.text: Capillary refill 4 seconds in the fingers of both hands (reference range less than 3 seconds); at 1800 it was 4 seconds
options.rationale: Capillary refill is unchanged and outside the range. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

options.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C); at 1800 it was 38.6 °C
options.rationale: The temperature has returned inside the range. It is one number and is judged with the rest of the trend.

options.text: Skin on both legs cool and mottled; at 1800 the skin was cool and mottled
options.rationale: Skin findings are part of the perfusion assessment. Unchanged cool, mottled skin is a persistent sign of poor perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend, not one number. Mentation, urine output, and temperature moving toward baseline count as response, and persistent signs of poor perfusion still call for escalation.
questions.strategy: The temperature drop is the eye catcher, and it pulls toward calling the whole picture a success. Judge each finding on its own trend: two perfusion signs have not moved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mentation, urine output, and temperature have moved toward baseline.
Capillary refill and skin findings are unchanged.
Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

options.text: Ask when the area appeared and about any recent injury, then assess warmth, pain, and use of the leg
options.rationale: Assessment begins with onset, recent injury, and illness history, followed by the physical findings. This gives the baseline.

options.text: Assess warmth, pain, and use of the leg, then report the area to the provider as an infection
options.rationale: The physical findings are needed, but redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and no history has been taken.

options.text: Ask when the area appeared and about any recent injury, then recheck the area tomorrow morning
options.rationale: The history is right, but the physical assessment is put off for a day and no baseline is recorded.

options.text: Mark the edge of the redness, then document the area as inflammation from a minor injury
options.rationale: Marking the edge helps later comparison, but no injury has been reported. Naming a cause before asking is a guess.

questions.takeaway: For a new area of redness, warmth, and swelling: ask about onset, recent injury, and illness history, then assess warmth, color, swelling, pain, and function to set the baseline.

steps.detail: No onset, no cause, no baseline.
Reporting infection, waiting a day, and naming a cause each go wrong.

questions.stem: A client bumped the left lower leg on a bed frame 2 days ago. Today an area on the left lower leg is warm, red, and swollen, and the client rates the pain 5 of 10. The skin over the area is intact. A family member says, "It is red and swollen, so it must be infected." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "These signs can come from the bump itself. I will mark the edge and look again tomorrow."
options.rationale: The explanation and the mark are right, but a day is a long gap and there is no commitment to report worsening.

options.text: "These signs can come from the bump itself. I will keep checking and report it if it worsens."
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow an injury without infection. The nurse says so and commits to reassessment and to reporting any worsening.

options.text: "These signs can come from the bump itself. I will report it if a fever develops."
options.rationale: The explanation is right, but worsening at the site is reported as well. The nurse does not wait for a fever.

options.text: "These signs usually mean that infection is starting, so I will ask for treatment to be safe."
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation can occur without infection. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and the nurse keeps assessing and reports worsening.
questions.strategy: Three options correctly say the bump can cause these signs. They differ in what comes next: look again tomorrow, wait for a fever, or keep checking and report worsening.

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: A bump 2 days ago, skin intact.
One leaves a day between checks and one waits for a fever.

steps.action: Keep the one that explains and reassesses

questions.nursesNote:
Yesterday 0800, day 3 after a bump to the left lower leg: red area 2 cm across, warm to touch, pain 3 of 10, walks to bathroom without help, skin intact, oral temperature 36.6 °C.

segments.text: Red area on left lower leg is 2 cm across
segments.rationale: The size of the redness matches yesterday's entry.

segments.text: Area is warm to touch
segments.rationale: Warmth is a cardinal sign and has not changed.

segments.text: Pain is 5 of 10
segments.rationale: Pain was 3 of 10 yesterday. It has risen, and a worsening sign is followed up.

segments.text: Walks to bathroom only with one person helping
segments.rationale: Yesterday the client walked to the bathroom without help. Functional ability has decreased from baseline.

segments.text: Skin over the area is intact
segments.rationale: Intact skin matches yesterday and is not a worsening finding.

segments.text: Oral temperature is 36.7 °C
segments.rationale: This reading is close to yesterday's 36.6 °C and does not cancel the two findings that are worse.

questions.takeaway: Assess warmth, color, swelling, pain, and functional ability, and compare each with baseline. Unchanged redness does not outweigh worse pain and lost function.
questions.strategy: The eye goes to the redness, which is unchanged. Line up each of today's findings with yesterday's entry: two of them are worse.

Pain 3 to 5 of 10, and walking alone to walking with help.

questions.stem: A client bumped the left lower leg 5 days ago and the skin is intact. Yesterday at 0800 the note read: red area 2 cm across, pain 5 of 10, walks to the bathroom with one person helping. Today at 0800 the red area is still 2 cm across, the client rates pain 7 of 10, and the client is unable to stand on the left leg. The client slept in a chair overnight with the left leg bent and says, "I just slept on it wrong. Please do not bother anyone about it." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Respect the client's request, document today's findings, and recheck the left leg in 4 hours
options.rationale: Listening to the client matters, but pain and function are clearly worse than baseline. A request not to bother anyone does not remove the duty to report worsening.

options.text: Give the ordered pain relief, reassess the pain in 1 hour, and report then if the client still cannot stand
options.rationale: Treating the pain is reasonable care, but it delays the report of two findings that are already clearly worse than baseline.

options.text: Report the rise in pain and the loss of standing now, and explain to the client why it needs to be reported
options.rationale: Pain has risen from 5 to 7 of 10 and the client can no longer stand on the left leg. Worsening is reported whatever the suspected cause, and the nurse tells the client why.

options.text: Ask the client to stand once more with help, and report only if the client is still unable to stand
options.rationale: The assessment already shows the change. Repeating it delays the report and adds nothing.

questions.takeaway: Changes from baseline that show worsening are reported. A client's explanation is heard and documented, and the report is still made.
questions.strategy: Three things pull toward waiting: the redness has not changed, the client offers another cause, and the client has asked the nurse not to report. The deciding cue is that pain and function are both worse than yesterday, and the nurse reports findings without having to settle the cause.

steps.detail: Redness same. Pain 5 to 7 of 10. Walking with help to unable to stand.
It is heard, but it does not change the findings.
Pain relief does not replace reporting a loss of function.

steps.action: Do not repeat what is known
steps.detail: Standing again only delays the report.

elimination.verdict: Report the rise in pain and the loss of standing now, and explain why.

questions.stem: A nurse is orienting a new nurse to the care of a client with a red, swollen area around a wound on the right heel. The client has eaten poorly for a month. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Which statement by the new nurse requires correction?

options.text: "I will compare what I find today with the earlier notes before I decide anything."
options.rationale: This is correct. Findings are compared with the client's baseline.

options.text: "A temperature inside the range does not tell me this wound is free of infection."
options.rationale: This sounds wrong but is correct. The nurse does not rely on fever alone; findings at the site and changes from baseline are assessed as well.

options.text: "The redness is the same size as yesterday, so the wound is the same as yesterday."
options.rationale: Redness is one finding. Swelling, pain, and functional ability are assessed and compared with baseline before the nurse can say nothing has changed.

options.text: "Poor intake of protein and vitamins for a month can slow the healing of this wound."
options.rationale: This is correct. Adequate protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and one unchanged finding does not establish that nothing changed. The nurse assesses every sign, including pain and function, compares with baseline, and does not rely on temperature alone.
questions.strategy: The question asks for the wrong statement. The one that sounds wrong, about temperature, is true; the one that sounds careful judges the whole wound by a single finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the statement that is not accurate.

steps.action: Test the statement that sounds wrong
steps.detail: A temperature inside the range does not rule out infection, so B is accurate.
C judges the whole wound by redness alone and skips swelling, pain, and function.
Comparing with earlier notes and linking nutrition to healing are accurate.

elimination.verdict: C. One unchanged finding does not show that the wound has not changed.
