questions.stem: A client has a wound on the right heel and has eaten poorly for a month. Yesterday at 0800 the note read: redness 1 cm around the wound, mild swelling, no drainage, pain 2 of 10. Today at 0800 the redness extends 3 cm around the wound, the swelling has increased, the dressing holds thick yellow drainage (pus), and the client rates pain 6 of 10. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. A new nurse says, "Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, so I will chart this as inflammation." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Agree, document the findings as expected inflammation, and compare the heel again at 2000
options.rationale: The rule is quoted correctly, but it no longer fits. There is more than redness and swelling here: the drainage is new, and the redness, swelling, and pain are all worse.

options.text: Report the wider redness, new thick yellow drainage, and higher pain now as findings that suggest infection
options.rationale: Redness has spread from 1 cm to 3 cm, pain has risen from 2 to 6 of 10, and thick yellow drainage is new. Pus is a sign of local infection, and worsening findings are reported.

options.text: Clean away the drainage, apply a fresh dressing, and report if drainage appears again by 2000
options.rationale: Wound care is appropriate, but waiting for the drainage to return delays the report of findings that are already worse.

options.text: Report the findings once the oral temperature rises above the 36.8 °C measured this morning
options.rationale: The nurse does not wait for a fever. The local findings have already changed.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Spreading redness, rising pain, and new pus are more than that: they are worsening findings that suggest infection and are reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The new nurse's rule is true and it is the trap. Ask what the stem adds beyond redness and swelling, and whether the findings match yesterday.

steps.detail: Redness 1 cm to 3 cm. Pain 2 to 6 of 10. Drainage: none to thick yellow.

steps.action: Test the rule against the stem
steps.detail: "Alone" no longer applies. Drainage is new.
For more drainage, or for a fever.
It states the findings and what they suggest.

elimination.verdict: Report the wider redness, new drainage, and higher pain as findings that suggest infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client twisted the right knee stepping off a curb 1 day ago. The skin over the knee is intact. The knee is warm, red, and swollen, and the client rates the pain 5 of 10. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C).

The findings at the right knee are best explained by [[1]].

The swelling at the knee develops because [[2]].

On reassessment, the nurse would treat [[3]] as a finding that requires follow up.

options.text: inflammation without infection, a protective response to the injury
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur after an injury without infection. A twisted knee with intact skin fits this.

options.text: infection, because warmth, redness, and swelling are all present
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: inflammation caused by microorganisms that entered at the time of injury
options.rationale: Inflammation is the right idea, but the skin is intact and nothing in the stem shows invasion by microorganisms.

options.text: an adaptive immune response directed at a specific antigen
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity. It is a rapid, broad response that needs no prior exposure.

options.text: fluid moves from the blood vessels into the tissue around the injury
options.rationale: In the vascular response, vessels dilate, blood flow increases, and fluid moves from the vessels into the tissue, causing swelling.

options.text: microorganisms multiply in the tissue around the injury
options.rationale: This describes infection. Swelling after an injury comes from fluid leaving the vessels.

options.text: blood vessels at the site narrow and hold fluid in the tissue
options.rationale: The vessels dilate in the vascular response. Narrowing does not explain swelling.

options.text: scar tissue forms and replaces the damaged tissue
options.rationale: Scar formation belongs to tissue repair, the last stage. It does not cause the early swelling.

options.text: redness that has spread beyond the edge marked yesterday
options.rationale: Findings are compared with baseline, and worsening is reported. Redness spreading beyond the marked edge is a change from baseline.

options.text: warmth and swelling that are still present 1 day later
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling are cardinal signs of inflammation. Still being present 1 day after the injury is expected, not worsening.

options.text: pain that is now 4 of 10
options.rationale: Pain was 5 of 10 at baseline. A lower rating is not a worsening finding.

options.text: an oral temperature of 37.0 °C, up from 36.8 °C yesterday
options.rationale: Both readings are inside the stated reference range of 36.1 to 37.2 °C. A change inside the range is not worsening.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation is a protective response that can follow an injury without infection. Swelling comes from fluid leaving dilated vessels, and only a change from baseline that shows worsening is followed up.
questions.strategy: Every blank has an option that sounds clinical but adds something the stem does not say. Check each against the stem: intact skin, a clear injury, and a temperature inside the stated range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A twisted knee with intact skin points to inflammation without infection.
Fluid moves from dilated vessels into the tissue.
Only the finding that has worsened from baseline needs follow up.
Warmth and swelling at day 1 are expected; a temperature change inside the reference range is not worsening.

elimination.verdict: Inflammation without infection; fluid moves from the vessels into the tissue; redness that has spread beyond the marked edge.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A nurse educator reviews findings from five clients with a new nurse. None of the clients has a temperature outside the reference range of 36.1 to 37.2 °C. Which findings suggest infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: A warm, swollen bruise on the left thigh 2 days after a fall, skin intact
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow an injury without infection, and the skin is intact.

options.text: Red, itchy skin on both hands after cleaning with a new chemical product without gloves, skin intact
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow exposure to an irritant. Redness alone does not establish infection.

options.text: A cut on the right index finger that is red, swollen, and now drains thick yellow fluid
options.rationale: Thick yellow drainage is pus. Pus at a site is a sign of local infection, not a finding of inflammation alone.

options.text: A blister on the right heel from new shoes, filled with clear fluid, covering skin unbroken
options.rationale: Blister formation is an example of inflammation without infection.

options.text: Redness around a sacral wound that has spread from 1 cm to 5 cm since yesterday, with pain rising from 3 to 6 of 10
options.rationale: Extended redness around a wound and rising pain are worsening findings that suggest infection, even with a temperature inside the reference range.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation can follow injury, an irritant, or infection. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, while pus or redness that spreads around a wound suggests it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A normal temperature is the trap: it is true for every client and settles nothing. Decide each finding by what is present at the site and whether it has changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A fall, a chemical, and new shoes are triggers that cause inflammation without infection.

steps.action: Look for more than redness and swelling
steps.detail: Pus and spreading redness point toward infection.
The temperature is in range for all five clients, so it separates none of them.

elimination.verdict: C, E.

questions.stem: A client admitted 2 days ago takes an immunosuppressant. The admission note includes a skin assessment of both arms. Today the client reports a painful, swollen area on the right forearm. The nurse has asked when the area appeared and whether the forearm was injured, and has assessed warmth, color, swelling, pain, and use of the right hand and forearm. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Report the area to the provider now as an infection, because the client takes an immunosuppressant
options.rationale: A report is right once worsening is shown, but swelling and pain alone do not establish infection, and the findings have not yet been compared with baseline.

options.text: Recheck the right forearm tomorrow morning to see whether the swollen area has spread further
options.rationale: Waiting a day skips the comparison the nurse can make now, and it delays reporting any change in a client whose immune protection may be reduced.

options.text: Document today's findings as the new baseline for the right forearm and continue routine care
options.rationale: Documenting is part of the process, but treating today as the new baseline skips the comparison with the admission skin assessment and could hide a change.

options.text: Compare today's findings with the right forearm findings recorded in the admission note
options.rationale: After the history and the physical assessment, the nurse compares findings with baseline. The comparison shows whether this is a change to document and report as worsening.

questions.takeaway: Ask about onset and injury; assess warmth, color, swelling, pain, and function; compare with baseline; then document and report worsening.
questions.strategy: The report is tempting to move up because the client takes an immunosuppressant. A report needs findings and a comparison, and the comparison is the step still missing.

steps.detail: History and the physical assessment are done.
Comparison with the admission note has not happened yet.
Reporting infection now skips the comparison and overcalls the finding; waiting until tomorrow delays it.
Calling today the new baseline skips the comparison with admission.

elimination.verdict: D. Compare with the admission findings, then document and report the worsening.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning closer assessment for clients on a medical unit whose immune protection may be reduced. Which clients does the nurse identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 6 week old infant admitted with a feeding problem
options.rationale: Infants have immature immune systems.

options.text: An 86 year old admitted after a fall who lives alone
options.rationale: Older adults face immunosenescence, which affects their ability to fight infections.

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained left ankle that is warm, red, and swollen
options.rationale: These are cardinal signs of inflammation after an injury. Inflammation is a protective response, not a factor that reduces immune protection.

options.text: A 41 year old who takes a daily antirejection drug after a kidney transplant
options.rationale: An antirejection drug suppresses the immune system, and immunosuppressants can affect immune function.

options.text: A 29 year old who received a measles vaccination 1 month ago
options.rationale: Vaccination produces artificial active immunity. It builds protection rather than reducing it.

options.text: A 52 year old who has eaten less than half of each meal for 1 month
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function.

questions.takeaway: Age and developmental stage, nutritional status, disease and overall health, medications, and environmental exposures affect immunity. Signs of inflammation and a recent vaccination do not reduce protection.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe the immune system working: a swollen ankle and a recent vaccination. Ask whether each option lowers protection or shows it in action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An infant and an 86 year old both qualify.
An antirejection drug and poor intake both lower protection.
An antirejection drug suppresses the immune system.

steps.action: Reject the immune system at work
steps.detail: Inflammation and vaccination are protective responses.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients. The oral temperature reference range is 36.1 to 37.2 °C. Which client does the nurse assess first?

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained left ankle; redness is 8 cm across and pain is 6 of 10, both the same as yesterday
options.rationale: The redness is large, but it and the pain match yesterday. Unchanged cardinal signs after an injury fit inflammation without infection.

options.text: A 58 year old with a right shin wound; redness grew from 2 to 3 cm and pain from 3 to 5 of 10 since yesterday
options.rationale: Redness and pain have both worsened since yesterday. A temperature is not needed before acting on a change at the site.

options.text: A 78 year old with a right hand wound and dementia; oral temperature 37.4 °C and confusion, both unchanged since admission yesterday
options.rationale: The reading is above the reference range and the client is confused, which pulls hard. The deciding cue is that both findings are unchanged since admission.

options.text: A 45 year old with a rash on both forearms after using a cleaning product; the rash is smaller than yesterday
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow an irritant, and a rash that is smaller than at baseline is not a worsening finding.

questions.takeaway: Priority goes to the client who has changed from baseline. A finding outside a range that has not changed is less urgent than a worsening one, and the nurse does not wait for fever.
questions.strategy: Two options pull hard: the only temperature above the range belongs to an older, confused client, while the other client has a modest change. The deciding cue is "unchanged since admission yesterday" against "since yesterday": unchanged findings wait, worsening findings come first.

steps.detail: Ankle unchanged, temperature and confusion unchanged, rash smaller, shin wound worse.

steps.action: Do not let one number decide
steps.detail: A temperature above range that has not changed is not new.
Assess the client whose findings have worsened.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client whose shin wound redness and pain have worsened since yesterday.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews findings for four clients on a medical unit. The oral temperature reference range is 36.1 to 37.2 °C. Which finding is best described as colonization?

options.text: A sore throat with swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck; oral temperature 38.6 °C
options.rationale: Pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy often accompany infection, and a temperature above the reference range adds a sign of systemic involvement. This is infection.

options.text: A leg wound grows methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA); redness spread 2 to 6 cm, pus; oral temperature 37.0 °C
options.rationale: An organism is present, as in colonization, but spreading redness and pus are signs of local infection. A temperature inside the range does not change that.

options.text: A urine culture from a long term catheter grows bacteria; urine clear, no pain, temperature 36.9 °C
options.rationale: Colonization means microorganisms are present in tissues without causing symptomatic disease. Bacteria were found, but nothing shows symptomatic disease.

options.text: Sneezing, clear nasal drainage, and swollen nasal tissue each spring; oral temperature 36.7 °C
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow exposure to an irritant. Allergic rhinitis is inflammation that occurs without infection and without an organism.

questions.takeaway: Finding an organism is not the same as infection. Colonization has an organism and no symptomatic disease; infection has an organism that multiplies and causes signs; inflammation can occur with no organism at all.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options name an organism on a culture. The catheter pulls toward infection, but decide by whether the site shows signs of disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the options with an organism
steps.detail: The leg wound and the urine culture both grew an organism.
The wound has spreading redness and pus: infection. The urine is clear with no pain: colonization.
The sore throat with a temperature above range is infection; the seasonal sneezing is inflammation without an organism.

elimination.verdict: C. Bacteria are present without symptomatic disease.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client was admitted yesterday with acute pancreatitis. Current findings: oral temperature 38.4 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C), heart rate 112 beats/min (reference range 60 to 100 beats/min), respiratory rate 22 breaths/min (reference range 12 to 20 breaths/min), and white blood cell (WBC) count 13,500 per mm3 (reference range 5000 to 10,000 per mm3). No source of infection has been found. Blood cultures drawn on admission show no growth so far. The client is alert and oriented, as on admission, oxygen saturation is 97% (reference range 95 to 100%), and urine output is 60 mL/hr (reference range at least 30 mL/hr). A new nurse says, "This meets SIRS criteria, so the client has sepsis." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "SIRS criteria are met here, so sepsis is present and the antimicrobial is given within 1 hour."
options.rationale: SIRS describes a widespread inflammatory response and can occur with noninfectious causes such as pancreatitis. SIRS alone does not establish sepsis.

options.text: "This is widespread inflammation. Sepsis also needs infection with organ dysfunction, not shown here."
options.rationale: Sepsis requires infection plus organ dysfunction. Mentation matches admission, oxygen saturation and urine output are inside their ranges, and no infection source has been found.

options.text: "Sepsis can be ruled out, because no organism has been found in the client's blood cultures at this point."
options.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

options.text: "These findings point to early sepsis, because the respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min is now above 20 breaths/min."
options.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min is concerning and is trended. Alone it does not show organ dysfunction when mentation, oxygen saturation, and urine output are inside their ranges.

questions.takeaway: SIRS is inflammation spread through the body, and pancreatitis can cause it without infection. Sepsis needs infection plus organ dysfunction, so look for new confusion, poor oxygenation, or falling urine output.
questions.strategy: Option D is the pull: a respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min is a sepsis cue on the slides. The deciding cue is that every marker of organ function in the stem, mentation, oxygen saturation, and urine output, is at baseline or inside its range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pancreatitis is a noninfectious cause of SIRS.
"Ruled out" ignores that sepsis is a clinical diagnosis.
Mentation at baseline, oxygen saturation 97%, urine output 60 mL/hr: none shown.
It is concerning and is trended, but one number does not establish sepsis.

elimination.verdict: SIRS alone is not sepsis; sepsis needs infection with organ dysfunction, and none is shown.

questions.stem: A client has a draining wound on the right foot that was cultured 3 days ago. Today the white blood cell (WBC) count is 16,800 per mm3 (reference range 5000 to 10,000 per mm3) and band neutrophils are 12% (reference range up to 5%). Oral temperature is 37.0 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Which statement by the nurse interprets these results accurately?

options.text: "The marrow is releasing immature neutrophils that cannot engulf the organism. I will read this with the wound findings and baseline now."
options.rationale: A left shift means more immature band neutrophils are circulating because the marrow cannot keep up with a continuing infection, and immature neutrophils cannot phagocytose. Results are interpreted with the assessment and baseline.

options.text: "The marrow is releasing immature neutrophils that cannot engulf the organism. I will act on this once the temperature is above 37.2 °C."
options.rationale: The interpretation is right, but infection can be present without fever, and the nurse does not rely on fever alone.

options.text: "Memory cells are forming that target the organism in the wound. I will read this with the wound findings and baseline now."
options.rationale: Memory cells come from lymphocytes, part of adaptive immunity. Band cells are immature neutrophils, part of innate defense.

options.text: "Memory cells are forming that target the organism in the wound. I will act on this once the temperature is above 37.2 °C."
options.rationale: This has two errors. Memory cells come from lymphocytes, part of adaptive immunity, while band cells are immature neutrophils. The nurse also does not wait for fever, because infection can be present without it.

questions.takeaway: A left shift means the marrow is sending out immature neutrophils that cannot phagocytose, a sign the body is losing ground to a continuing infection. Read the results now with the wound and the baseline, not alone and not by temperature.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option has an interpretation and an action. Judge each half on its own: two options name the right cell, two take the right action, and only one gets both.

steps.detail: Bands are immature neutrophils, which cannot phagocytose.
Memory belongs to lymphocytes, which removes C and D.
Waiting for fever removes B and D; reading the result with the wound and baseline now fits A.

elimination.verdict: A. Immature neutrophils signal a marrow that cannot keep up, and the result is read now with the wound and baseline.

questions.stem: A client was admitted 2 days ago with an infected wound on the left lower leg. At 0800 the client was alert and oriented, respiratory rate was 18 breaths/min, and heart rate was 88 beats/min. At 1400 the client is restless and asks where they are. Respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min (reference range 12 to 20 breaths/min), heart rate is 118 beats/min (reference range 60 to 100 beats/min), and urine output is 40 mL over the past 2 hours (reference range at least 30 mL/hr). Oral temperature is 37.1 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the oral temperature in 1 hour and notify the provider if it rises above 37.2 °C
options.rationale: Notifying the provider is the right idea, but tying it to fever is the error. New confusion, a rising respiratory rate, and falling urine output are already present, and the nurse does not wait for fever.

options.text: Mark the edge of the wound redness now and compare it at the next dressing change
options.rationale: Comparing the site with baseline is right in general, but the changes now are in breathing, mentation, and urine output, and they cannot wait.

options.text: Explain the unit routine to ease anxiety, then reassess the restlessness in 1 hour
options.rationale: Anxiety does not explain urine output below its reference range. New confusion is compared with the 0800 baseline and treated as a sepsis cue.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate rapid response now for possible sepsis from the wound
options.rationale: An infected wound plus new confusion, a respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min, and urine output below range are early cues of sepsis. When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is an immune response to infection that has become uncontrolled and disrupts organ function. New confusion, faster breathing, and falling urine output are the early cues, and a temperature inside the range does not delay escalation.
questions.strategy: The temperature inside the range is the trap. Name the problem from the changes since 0800: mentation, respiratory rate, heart rate, and urine output.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alert to restless and disoriented; respiratory rate 18 to 28; heart rate 88 to 118; urine output 20 mL/hr.
An infected wound with organ dysfunction cues points to possible sepsis.
Waiting for fever, for the next dressing change, or for an hour of reassurance all postpone escalation.
Escalate now to the provider or the rapid response process.

elimination.verdict: D. Possible sepsis calls for immediate escalation, without waiting for fever.

questions.stem: A client reports pain in both knees for 2 weeks. Both knees are warm and swollen, and the client rates the pain 5 of 10. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 42 mm/hr (reference range 0 to 20 mm/hr). The white blood cell (WBC) count is 7600 per mm3 (reference range 5000 to 10,000 per mm3), and oral temperature is 36.9 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The raised ESR shows infection in both knees, so I will report it before I assess further."
options.rationale: The ESR rises with inflammation and with infection. It does not name a cause or a location, and the knees have not yet been assessed.

options.text: "The WBC count and temperature are in range, so the ESR shows inflammation without infection."
options.rationale: Infection can be present without fever, and a WBC count inside the range does not rule it out. The ESR cannot separate the two.

options.text: "The ESR shows inflammation or infection somewhere, so I will ask about onset, then assess each knee."
options.rationale: An ESR above 20 mm/hr indicates inflammation or infection somewhere in the body. Assessment begins with onset, recent injury, and illness history, then the findings at each site.

options.text: "The ESR shows inflammation or infection somewhere, so I will apply ice and recheck pain in 1 hour."
options.rationale: The interpretation is right, but comfort measures come after the history and the assessment of each knee. Assessment comes before intervention.

questions.takeaway: An ESR above 20 mm/hr says inflammation or infection is present somewhere in the body. It cannot say which, so the nurse reads it together with the history and the assessment of the site.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and B each turn a lab value into a conclusion about cause. Ask what the ESR can tell you: that something is inflamed, not why. Then choose the option that gathers more data before acting.

steps.action: Read the value against its range
steps.detail: 42 mm/hr is above 0 to 20 mm/hr.

steps.action: Reject the leap to a cause
steps.detail: The ESR rises with both inflammation and infection, so it cannot confirm infection (A) or rule it out (B).
C and D read the ESR correctly; D intervenes before the knees are assessed.
History, then a focused assessment of each knee.

elimination.verdict: C. The ESR shows inflammation or infection without naming which, so the nurse takes the history and assesses each knee.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a central venous catheter in the right upper chest. Today the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 400 per mm3 (reference range 1500 to 8000 per mm3); the provider reviewed it at 0800 and neutropenic precautions are in place. At the catheter site the skin is pink 0.5 cm around the insertion point, there is no drainage, and pain at the site is 4 of 10, up from 1 of 10 yesterday. Oral temperature is 37.0 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document the site as free of infection, since there is no drainage and the pink area is only 0.5 cm
options.rationale: Little redness and no drainage would be reassuring with an ANC in range. With an ANC of 400 per mm3, few neutrophils reach the site, so these signs cannot be relied on.

options.text: Report the new site pain now, since a low neutrophil count mutes the redness and pus of infection
options.rationale: Pus forms from dead WBCs, and the ANC of 400 per mm3 is far below range. Local signs are blunted, so the rise in pain from 1 to 4 of 10 is reported as a change from baseline.

options.text: Report the ANC of 400 per mm3 now, since a count this low places the client at high risk for infection
options.rationale: The ANC is low, but the provider reviewed it at 0800 and neutropenic precautions are in place. The change that has not been reported is the rise in site pain.

options.text: Recheck the site and temperature in 4 hours, since a fever would show whether the site is infected
options.rationale: Infection can be present without fever when immunity is low, so waiting for fever delays the report of pain that has already risen from 1 to 4 of 10.

questions.takeaway: Pus and much of the redness of infection come from neutrophils at the site. When the ANC is very low, those signs are muted, so a smaller change such as new pain is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is partly covered in Reading (Iggy) and completed by standard NCLEX teaching.
questions.strategy: B and C both escalate. The deciding cue is that the provider reviewed the ANC at 0800 and precautions are in place, so the unreported change is the pain rising from 1 to 4 of 10.

steps.action: Read the ANC against its range
steps.detail: 400 per mm3 against 1500 to 8000 per mm3.
Few neutrophils means little pus and muted redness.
Pain 1 to 4 of 10 since yesterday.
The ANC has already been reviewed and acted on.
Infection can be present without fever when immunity is low (Iggy), so waiting for fever delays the report.

elimination.verdict: Report the new site pain now; a low ANC blunts redness and pus.

questions.stem: A client, 81 years old, is admitted with vomiting for 2 days. Blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg (normal is below 120/80 mm Hg), and heart rate is 112 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute). The nurse calculates the mean arterial pressure and compares it with the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to maintain perfusion of the major body organs. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: 54 mm Hg, which is below the level needed to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: Mean arterial pressure is the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3: (78 + 84) divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg, which is under 60 mm Hg, so perfusion of the major organs is at risk.

options.text: 60 mm Hg, which is at the lower edge of the level needed for organ perfusion
options.rationale: This is the simple average of 78 and 42. The diastolic pressure is counted twice because the cycle spends more time in diastole, so the true value is lower.

options.text: 66 mm Hg, which is within the level needed to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: This doubles the systolic pressure instead of the diastolic pressure: (156 + 42) divided by 3. The heart rate of 112 beats per minute is not part of the formula and does not raise the value.

options.text: 36 mm Hg, which is far below the level needed to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: The interpretation that perfusion is at risk is right, but 36 mm Hg is the systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure, which is the pulse pressure, not the mean arterial pressure.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure equals the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3. A value of 60 to 70 mm Hg is necessary to maintain perfusion of the major body organs, so anything under 60 mm Hg puts them at risk.
questions.strategy: Write the formula before you look at the choices. The wrong numbers come from the common slips: averaging the two pressures, doubling the wrong one, or subtracting them. Then check the interpretation against 60 to 70 mm Hg.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 42 times 2 is 84.

steps.action: Add the systolic and divide by 3
steps.detail: 78 plus 84 is 162; 162 divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg.
54 mm Hg is below 60 to 70 mm Hg, so perfusion is at risk.
60 is the simple average, 66 doubles the systolic, and 36 is the pulse pressure.

elimination.verdict: A. 54 mm Hg, below the level needed to perfuse the major organs.

questions.scenario: A nurse completes admission assessments for several clients aged 76 to 88 years. None of these clients has a known heart disease.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the age related change in the cardiovascular system that best explains it.

rows.text: A soft murmur at the apex in a client who reports no shortness of breath
rows.rationale: With age the mitral and aortic valves calcify. A murmur may be detected before any other symptom appears.

rows.text: Resting heart rate 56 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), with occasional premature ventricular contractions on the monitor
rows.rationale: Pacemaker cells decrease in number and conduction time increases. A rate below 60 beats per minute and premature ventricular contractions are common in older adults.

rows.text: Heart rate rises only to 96 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute) during a walk in the hallway, and the client stops to rest after 20 meters
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume and cardiac output during exercise, and the maximum heart rate with exercise is lower. The result is activity intolerance.

rows.text: Dizziness each time the client moves from lying to standing
rows.rationale: Less sensitive baroreceptors do not adjust the pressure quickly when position changes, which causes orthostatic dizziness.

rows.text: Lightheadedness 30 minutes after lunch, with a seated blood pressure of 98/60 mm Hg (normal is below 120/80 mm Hg) compared with 132/78 mm Hg before lunch
rows.rationale: A drop in pressure after eating is a postprandial change. It comes from the same less sensitive baroreceptors as the orthostatic change, not from the valves or the ventricle.

rows.text: During an exercise test, ejection fraction falls to 48% (reference 55% to 70%), although it was 62% at rest
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume, ejection fraction, and cardiac output during exercise, so the heart is less able to meet increased oxygen demands.

questions.takeaway: Five areas change with age: the valves calcify, pacemaker cells decrease, the left ventricle grows larger and stiffer, the large arteries stiffen, and the baroreceptors lose sensitivity. Each change has its own finding to assess.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Link each finding to the structure that produces it. Pressure drops with position or meals belong to the baroreceptors; a limited response to activity belongs to the left ventricle; rate and premature beats belong to the conduction system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A murmur with no symptoms points to calcified valves.
Below 60 with premature beats points to fewer pacemaker cells.
A limited rise in rate with early fatigue points to the left ventricle.
Both the positional and the after meal drops come from the baroreceptors.
A fall in ejection fraction with activity points to the stiff, enlarged left ventricle.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac valves; conduction system; left ventricle; baroreceptors; baroreceptors; left ventricle.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: A client, 79 years old, has been on bed rest for 3 days and takes a diuretic. Before the first walk to the bathroom, the nurse checks orthostatic vital signs. After 3 minutes supine: blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats per minute. After 1 minute standing: blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, heart rate 80 beats per minute. Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mm Hg, and the reference range for heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute. The client reports no dizziness. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: No orthostatic change, because the systolic pressure fell by less than 20 mm Hg
options.rationale: The systolic fall of 16 mm Hg is under 20 mm Hg, but the definition is met by either pressure. The diastolic pressure fell 12 mm Hg.

options.text: No orthostatic change, because the client reports no dizziness on standing
options.rationale: Dizziness is observed and recorded, but the definition rests on the measured changes. The absence of symptoms does not cancel a diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension, because the standing systolic pressure is below 120 mm Hg
options.rationale: A standing systolic value below 120 mm Hg is not the test. Orthostatic hypotension is judged by the size of the fall from supine to standing.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension, because the diastolic fell 12 mm Hg as the rate rose
options.rationale: The diastolic pressure fell from 82 to 70 mm Hg, a fall of 12 mm Hg, and the heart rate rose from 70 to 80, about 14%. This meets the definition.

questions.takeaway: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall of more than 20 mm Hg systolic or more than 10 mm Hg diastolic, with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate. Either pressure can meet it, and the client does not have to feel dizzy.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Option A is the defensible trap: the systolic fall is under 20 mm Hg. The cue that decides is the diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg. Calculate both pressures and the heart rate change before you choose.

steps.detail: Systolic 134 to 118 is 16 mm Hg; diastolic 82 to 70 is 12 mm Hg; heart rate 70 to 80 is about 14%.
More than 10 mm Hg diastolic with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate is met.
A and B say no change; C and D say orthostatic hypotension. The measurements place the answer in the second pair.
C reaches the right label for the wrong reason; D names the fall that meets the definition.

elimination.verdict: D. The diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg with a 14% rise in heart rate meets the definition.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, comes to the clinic for a cardiovascular risk assessment. Which findings are modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease? Select all that apply.

options.text: Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years
options.rationale: Cigarette smoking is a modifiable risk factor and a major risk factor for coronary artery disease. This history is recorded as 30 pack years.

options.text: Body mass index 33 kg/m² (reference 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m²)
options.rationale: A body mass index above 30 kg/m² is obesity, a modifiable risk factor.

options.text: A parent had a myocardial infarction at 52 years of age
options.rationale: Family history matters and is part of the history, but it is a nonmodifiable risk factor.

options.text: Walks for 20 minutes once each week
options.rationale: This is far below 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week. Physical inactivity is a modifiable risk factor.

options.text: Reports feeling angry and hostile whenever there is a wait
options.rationale: Psychological factors such as anger and hostility are modifiable risk factors.

options.text: Is 58 years of age
options.rationale: The risk of coronary artery disease rises with age, but age is a nonmodifiable risk factor.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risk factors are lifestyle habits: smoking, physical inactivity, obesity, and psychological factors such as stress, anger, and hostility. Age, sex assigned at birth, ethnic origin, and family history are nonmodifiable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding whether the client could change it. Family history and age both raise risk, which makes them tempting, but neither can be changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client can stop: modifiable.
Both can change: modifiable.
Psychological factors are modifiable.
Both raise risk but cannot be changed.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a client, 72 years old, who is seen for fatigue. Heart rate is 84 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute) and regular. Which findings require further assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Point of maximal impulse palpated at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
options.rationale: This is the expected location of the point of maximal impulse.

options.text: An extra sound heard just after S2, during rapid ventricular filling
options.rationale: This is an S3. It may be normal under 35 years of age, but at 72 it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.

options.text: S1 and S2 heard clearly
options.rationale: S1 and S2 are the normal heart sounds.

options.text: Skin warm and pink on both hands
options.rationale: Warm, pink skin is an expected finding of skin color and temperature.

options.text: A whooshing sound heard between S1 and S2 at the apex, not recorded at the last visit
options.rationale: A whooshing sound between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur from turbulent flow, and it is new since the last visit.

options.text: Radial pulses equal on the right and left
options.rationale: Pulses that are equal on both sides are expected.

questions.takeaway: An S3 may be normal before 35 years of age but in an older adult may mean decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure. A murmur is a whooshing sound from turbulent flow, and a systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2.
questions.strategy: The S3 is the trap: it can be normal, so students leave it unselected. Read the client's age. At 72 the same sound points to the ventricle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Point of maximal impulse location, S1 and S2, skin, and pulses are all expected.

steps.action: Read the age with the S3
steps.detail: At 72 years an S3 is not expected.
The systolic murmur was not present at the last visit.

elimination.verdict: B, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 64 years old, has had hypertension for 10 years. Blood pressure today is 158/96 mm Hg (normal is below 120/80 mm Hg). While auscultating at the apex with the bell, the nurse hears a short, low pitched extra sound just before S1. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: An S3 gallop, reflecting decreased ventricular compliance from long standing hypertension
options.rationale: An S3 can also reflect decreased compliance, but it is heard during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. A sound just before S1 is timed to atrial contraction.

options.text: An S4 gallop, reflecting a stiff, noncompliant ventricle from long standing hypertension
options.rationale: An S4 is heard during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. It may occur with hypertension.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub from movement of an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: A friction rub comes from an inflamed pericardium. It is not tied to atrial contraction, and nothing in the stem suggests pericarditis.

options.text: A diastolic murmur from turbulent blood flow through a narrowed valve
options.rationale: A murmur is a whooshing or swishing sound from turbulent flow, not a short, low pitched extra sound.

questions.takeaway: S3 comes during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. S4 comes during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle, as seen with hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial infarction, or advancing age.
questions.strategy: A and B give the same cause, so the cause cannot decide. Time the sound: just before S1 is atrial contraction, which is an S4.

steps.detail: Just before S1, which is atrial contraction.
A is an S3 after S2; B is an S4 before S1.
A rub comes from the pericardium, and a murmur is whooshing.

elimination.verdict: B. A sound just before S1 is an S4, which fits a stiff ventricle from long standing hypertension.

questions.stem: During a procedure, a small air bubble enters a pulmonary vein of a client. The client's family asks how air in the lungs could reach the brain. Which sequence correctly lists the structures the air would pass through?

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: Blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve toward the arteries of the head.

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left atrium, tricuspid valve, left ventricle, pulmonic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: The chambers are in the right order, but both valves belong to the right side of the heart. On the left side the atrioventricular valve is the mitral valve and the semilunar valve is the aortic valve.

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left ventricle, mitral valve, left atrium, pulmonic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: Two errors. The chambers are reversed, because the pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium, and the pulmonic valve leads from the right ventricle to the lungs, not from the left ventricle.

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left ventricle, tricuspid valve, left atrium, aortic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: Two errors. The chambers are reversed, because the pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium, and the tricuspid valve sits on the right side of the heart, not between the left chambers.

questions.takeaway: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve to the arteries of the head, arms, and lower body.
questions.strategy: Start where blood from the lungs enters the heart, then alternate chamber and valve. On the left side the atrioventricular valve is the mitral and the semilunar valve is the aortic. Check each link on its own: chamber order, then each valve.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blood from the lungs enters through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, so the atrium comes before the ventricle. Eliminate C and D.
Mitral between the left chambers, aortic leaving the left ventricle. Tricuspid and pulmonic belong to the right side. Eliminate B.

elimination.verdict: A. Pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, arteries of the head.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A nurse auscultating a client, 66 years old, hears a murmur that falls between S1 and S2. Which events of the cardiac cycle are taking place while this murmur is heard? Select all that apply.

options.text: The aortic and pulmonic valves are open
options.rationale: Between S1 and S2 is ventricular ejection, when the aortic and pulmonic valves open.

options.text: The ventricles eject blood into the arteries
options.rationale: This interval is systole. The ventricles eject blood and ventricular pressure peaks.

options.text: The mitral and tricuspid valves are closed
options.rationale: The mitral and tricuspid valves close at S1 and do not open again until ventricular filling, after S2.

options.text: The ventricles fill as the mitral and tricuspid valves open
options.rationale: Ventricular filling with the mitral and tricuspid valves open happens in diastole, between S2 and the next S1.

options.text: The atria contract while the P wave appears
options.rationale: Atrial contraction with the P wave comes at the end of diastole, before S1.

options.text: The aortic and pulmonic valves close to make the second sound
options.rationale: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves is S2 itself, which ends this interval. It does not happen during the murmur.

questions.takeaway: S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves and starts systole. Between S1 and S2 the aortic and pulmonic valves are open and the ventricles eject. S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves and starts diastole, when the ventricles fill.
questions.strategy: Picture the interval as systole. Anything that belongs to filling, atrial contraction, or the closing that makes S2 belongs outside it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Between S1 and S2 is ventricular ejection, which is systole.
Aortic and pulmonic open; mitral and tricuspid closed.
Ventricular filling and atrial contraction come after S2 or before S1.
The closing that makes S2 ends the interval.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client has a clot blocking a deep vein in the right calf. The right calf is swollen, and the right foot is warm and pink with a pedal pulse equal to the left. Which function of the vascular system is directly impaired in the right leg?

options.text: Returning blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart
options.rationale: The primary function of the venous system is to complete the circulation by returning blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart. A blocked vein impairs this.

options.text: Delivering oxygen and nutrients from the heart to the tissues
options.rationale: This is the arterial system's function. The warm, pink foot with an equal pulse shows that arterial delivery is working.

options.text: Draining tissue fluid from the swollen calf back to the circulation through lymphatic flow
options.rationale: The calf swells because blood cannot return past the clot, not because lymphatic vessels are blocked. The structure that is directly impaired is the vein.

options.text: Carrying cell wastes from the tissues to the excretory organs
options.rationale: The vascular system does carry wastes, but the specific function lost when a vein is blocked is the return of blood to the heart.

questions.takeaway: The arterial system delivers oxygen and nutrients to body tissues. The venous system completes the circulation by returning blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart.
questions.strategy: Match the blocked vessel to its job. The warm, pink foot and equal pulse tell you the arteries are delivering, so the problem is return.

steps.detail: The clot is in a vein.
Return blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart.
A warm, pink foot with an equal pulse shows that delivery is intact.

elimination.verdict: A. A blocked vein impairs the return of blood to the right side of the heart.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client is admitted after blood loss from a fall. Heart rate is 125 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), and stroke volume is 32 mL per beat (reference 60 to 100 mL per beat). The reference range for cardiac output is 3 to 6 L/min. Which statement about this client's cardiac output is accurate?

options.text: It is 4.0 L/min, which shows the blood loss has not yet affected the heart
options.rationale: The number is correct, but the low stroke volume shows the blood loss has affected the heart. The output is held up only by the fast rate.

options.text: It is below range, because a stroke volume under 60 mL always lowers output
options.rationale: Output depends on both factors. A fast heart rate can offset a low stroke volume, and here 125 times 32 mL gives 4.0 L/min.

options.text: It is 4.0 L/min, kept in range by the fast rate offsetting low stroke volume
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume: 125 times 32 mL is 4,000 mL, or 4.0 L/min. The fast rate is offsetting the low stroke volume.

options.text: It cannot be judged until the heart rate is back below 100 beats per minute
options.rationale: Cardiac output can be calculated at any heart rate with the formula.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped from the left ventricle per minute, equal to heart rate times stroke volume. When stroke volume falls, a faster heart rate can keep output within range.
questions.strategy: Two options give the right number; only one gives the right meaning. A normal output with a low stroke volume and a fast rate means the heart is offsetting, not unaffected.

steps.detail: 125 times 32 mL is 4,000 mL per minute, or 4.0 L/min.
B says always; output depends on both factors.
Both say 4.0 L/min; only C explains why it is within range.

elimination.verdict: C. The fast heart rate is offsetting the low stroke volume.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: A client has blood pressure 186/108 mm Hg (normal is below 120/80 mm Hg) and arteries narrowed by long standing hypertension. Heart rate is 88 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute). Which statement best explains the effect on the left ventricle?

options.text: Preload rises, so the stretched muscle fibers contract with less force
options.rationale: Preload is the stretch from the volume in the ventricle at the end of diastole. High arterial pressure and narrow vessels change the resistance, not the filling volume.

options.text: Afterload rises, so the stretched fibers contract harder and stroke volume rises
options.rationale: Afterload does rise, but a stronger contraction from added stretch is Starling's law, which describes preload. A rise in afterload without compensation lowers stroke volume.

options.text: Preload falls, because high arterial pressure blocks blood returning to the heart
options.rationale: Preload depends on blood returning from the venous and pulmonary systems. Arterial pressure is the resistance against ejection.

options.text: Afterload rises, so stroke volume can fall unless the heart compensates
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. It rises with arterial pressure and narrow vessels, and a rise without compensation lowers stroke volume.

questions.takeaway: Preload is the stretch of the muscle fibers from the volume in the ventricle at the end of diastole. Afterload is the resistance the ventricle pumps against, which rises with arterial pressure and narrower vessels and can lower stroke volume.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the cue first: high pressure and narrow arteries describe resistance, which is afterload. Then pick the effect: more afterload means more resistance to eject against, so stroke volume can fall.

steps.detail: High arterial pressure and narrowed arteries are resistance.
A and C both blame volume, the shared wrong fact.
B and D both say afterload rises; only D gives the correct effect on stroke volume.

elimination.verdict: D. Higher afterload makes the ventricle work harder and can lower stroke volume.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.scenario: A client, 61 years old, arrives at the emergency department with pressure in the chest that began 5 hours ago and is now 6 of 10. Blood pressure 146/90 mm Hg (normal is below 120/80 mm Hg), heart rate 104 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20 breaths per minute). The point of care troponin I is 0.48 ng/mL (reference below 0.03 ng/mL).
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Notify the provider of the troponin result now
options.rationale: A troponin I above 0.03 ng/mL indicates myocardial injury or infarction and is reported at once.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: Troponin is evaluated together with the symptoms and ECG changes, and a 12 lead ECG is obtained for chest pain.

options.text: Prepare the client for an exercise ECG to look for silent disease
options.rationale: An exercise ECG stops when chest pain appears. This client has chest pressure now and a troponin showing injury.

options.text: Wait for the repeat troponin before reporting the first result
options.rationale: Repeat testing is planned, but a value this far above the reference is reported now, not after the next result.

options.text: Walk the client to the restroom before testing begins
options.rationale: Activity raises the heart's oxygen demand in a client with ongoing chest pressure and evidence of injury.

options.text: Myocardial injury
options.rationale: Troponin is a heart muscle protein released into the blood when heart muscle is injured. A value above the reference with ongoing chest pressure points to myocardial injury.

options.text: Pericarditis from an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: Pericarditis may produce a friction rub, but the troponin result points to injury of the heart muscle.

options.text: Elevated serum lipids
options.rationale: Lipids estimate long term risk. No lipid result is given, and they do not explain an acute rise in troponin.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension
options.rationale: No positional blood pressure change is described, and the pressure is above normal.

options.text: Troponin repeated in 3 to 6 hours
options.rationale: After the first troponin, levels are assessed again in 3 to 6 hours.

options.text: Chest pressure rating
options.rationale: The pain rating tracks whether the ischemic pain continues or eases.

options.text: Total cholesterol level
options.rationale: Cholesterol guides long term risk reduction, not the course of acute injury.

options.text: Location of the point of maximal impulse
options.rationale: The point of maximal impulse is part of the physical assessment but does not track acute injury.

questions.takeaway: A troponin T or I above its reference indicates myocardial injury or infarction. Report it, obtain an ECG, and repeat troponin in 3 to 6 hours while tracking the pain.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the condition from the troponin result with the ongoing pressure, then choose actions that treat it as injury now and parameters that follow its course over hours.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.48 ng/mL is far above the reference of below 0.03 ng/mL.
Myocardial injury.
Report now and obtain a 12 lead ECG.
Repeat troponin in 3 to 6 hours and the chest pressure rating.

elimination.verdict: Myocardial injury; notify the provider and obtain a 12 lead ECG; monitor the repeat troponin and the chest pressure rating.

questions.stem: A client, 55 years old, arrives at the emergency department 40 minutes after chest pressure began while shoveling snow. The pressure is now 5 of 10. The point of care troponin I is 0.01 ng/mL (reference below 0.03 ng/mL). The client says, "The blood test is normal, so I want to go home." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Your troponin is normal, so an exercise ECG is next to look for hidden disease."
options.rationale: An exercise ECG does detect silent coronary disease, but it stops when chest pain appears. This client still has pressure rated 5 of 10.

options.text: "Troponin can take hours to rise, so it will be rechecked in 3 to 6 hours here."
options.rationale: The pressure began only 40 minutes ago. Troponin is repeated in 3 to 6 hours, so one early normal value does not rule out injury.

options.text: "Your first troponin is normal; an ECG will be done so the provider can decide about discharge."
options.rationale: An ECG is part of the evaluation, but this response presents one normal troponin as reassuring. Only 40 minutes have passed, so the troponin is repeated in 3 to 6 hours before injury can be excluded.

options.text: "Troponin stays raised a long time, so a normal level means it is not your heart."
options.rationale: Troponin stays raised for a long time after injury, which helps clients who arrive hours later. It does not mean an early normal value excludes injury.

questions.takeaway: Troponin is the preferred marker of heart muscle injury and is repeated 3 to 6 hours after the first result. A single normal value soon after symptoms begin does not rule out injury.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: B and C both keep the client for evaluation. The cue that decides is time: 40 minutes after onset, one normal troponin cannot exclude injury, so the repeat in 3 to 6 hours is what the client needs to hear.

steps.detail: 40 minutes since onset, with pressure still at 5 of 10.
D treats one normal troponin as ruling out injury, and A stresses the heart during ongoing pain.
C reassures with one early value; B explains why the marker is repeated.

elimination.verdict: B. One early normal troponin does not rule out injury, so it is repeated in 3 to 6 hours.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for several clients who returned within the past 2 hours from a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery. Before each procedure, the right dorsalis pedis pulse was present and equal to the left. Which findings require immediate action? Select all that apply.

options.text: New chest pressure rated 4 of 10
options.rationale: Chest pain after catheterization is a critical rescue finding. The nurse stays with the client and obtains a 12 lead ECG.

options.text: Urine output 240 mL over the past hour (reference at least 30 mL per hour)
options.rationale: The contrast acts as an osmotic diuretic, so a high urine output is expected. The nurse keeps oral and intravenous fluids going so the contrast is excreted.

options.text: The right dorsalis pedis pulse is now absent, and the right foot is cool and pale
options.rationale: A dramatic change in the pulses of the affected limb is a critical rescue finding. The rapid response team or provider is contacted at once.

options.text: Blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg (normal is below 120/80 mm Hg) and heart rate 80 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), both matching the values before the procedure
options.rationale: The values match the client's own baseline, so they do not signal bleeding or another complication.

options.text: The right foot is warm and pink, with a right dorsalis pedis pulse equal to the left
options.rationale: Pulses, temperature, and color in the affected limb match the baseline, which shows circulation below the site is intact.

options.text: Firm swelling that is growing under the right groin dressing
options.rationale: A forming hematoma calls for steady, firm pressure on the site and the rapid response team or provider at once.

questions.takeaway: After catheterization, check the site and the limb below it with every vital sign check. Chest pain, dysrhythmias, bleeding, hematoma, or a dramatic change in the limb pulses call for the rapid response team or provider at once. High urine output from the contrast is expected.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with the baseline from before the procedure. Anything that matches the baseline or follows from the contrast is expected; anything new at the site, in the limb, or in the chest is acted on now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New chest pressure is a critical rescue finding.
Osmotic diuresis from contrast is expected.
A lost pulse with a cool, pale foot is a dramatic change; a pulse matching baseline is expected.
Growing firm swelling is a hematoma.

elimination.verdict: A, C, F.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery at 1300. At 1100 the nurse reviews the checklist. The client ate toast at 0600, drank clear apple juice at 0930, and took the usual warfarin dose at 0800. The signed consent is complete, and the client reports no allergies. Which action by the nurse is most important?

options.text: Report that the client drank apple juice this morning, so the procedure is delayed
options.rationale: Clear liquids are allowed up to 2 hours before the procedure. The juice at 0930 was 3.5 hours before 1300.

options.text: Report that the client ate toast this morning, so the procedure is delayed
options.rationale: Solids are held for 6 hours before the procedure. The toast at 0600 was 7 hours before 1300.

options.text: Report the warfarin dose taken at 0800 to the provider before the procedure
options.rationale: Warfarin and other oral anticoagulants are held when the femoral artery will be used, because of the bleeding risk at the site.

options.text: Ask whether the client has ever reacted to iodine based contrast before the procedure
options.rationale: Contrast allergy is questioned before the procedure, and the client already reports no allergies. A warfarin dose before femoral arterial access is the finding that puts the client at risk and must reach the provider.

questions.takeaway: Before catheterization, clear liquids are allowed up to 2 hours before and solids are held for 6 hours. Warfarin and other oral anticoagulants are held when the femoral artery will be used, so a dose taken that morning is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The juice is the defensible trap because many clients are told to take nothing by mouth. Count the hours: 0930 to 1300 is 3.5 hours, beyond the 2 hour limit for clear liquids. The femoral access is the cue that makes the warfarin the problem.

steps.detail: Juice 3.5 hours before and toast 7 hours before are both within the rules.
A and B both delay the procedure for intake that meets the rules.
The femoral artery will be used, so warfarin should have been held.
Useful, but the client reports no allergies; the warfarin is the unaddressed risk.

elimination.verdict: C. Warfarin is held when femoral access is planned, so the morning dose is reported.

questions.stem: A nurse on a cardiac unit reviews findings documented for several clients who have heart failure. Which findings indicate right sided heart failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Neck veins distended with the head of the bed raised to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Jugular venous distention reflects systemic venous congestion. When the right ventricle fails, blood backs up into the systemic veins.

options.text: Sleeps on 3 pillows and becomes short of breath within minutes of lying flat
options.rationale: Orthopnea comes from pulmonary congestion. Blood backs up into the lungs when the left ventricle fails, so this is a left sided finding.

options.text: New confusion, with cool hands and feet bilaterally
options.rationale: Confusion and cool extremities reflect decreased cardiac output and decreased perfusion, a left sided pattern.

options.text: Reports no appetite and nausea at meals, with a liver edge palpable below the right costal margin
options.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, and hepatomegaly come from systemic venous congestion of the liver and gut, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Abdominal girth up 4 cm in 3 days with a distended, tight abdomen
options.rationale: Ascites and abdominal distention reflect systemic venous congestion, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Urine output 22 mL per hour for 3 hours (reference at least 30 mL per hour)
options.rationale: Lower urine output is a decreased cardiac output finding. The failing left ventricle sends less blood to the kidneys.

questions.takeaway: Left sided failure backs blood into the lungs and lowers output: dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, cough, fatigue, tachycardia, confusion, cool extremities, lower urine output. Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins: dependent edema, JVD, weight gain, ascites, hepatomegaly, anorexia and nausea.
questions.strategy: Ask where the blood is backing up. Lungs or low output points left. Neck veins, belly, liver, and legs point right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distended neck veins, ascites, and the liver and gut findings are systemic congestion: right. Orthopnea is lung congestion: left.
Low urine output, confusion, and cool extremities come from decreased cardiac output: left.
Nausea and poor appetite sound like low perfusion of the gut, but they come from venous congestion: right.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.nursesNote: Client admitted with heart failure. Reports shortness of breath walking to the bathroom and waking at night gasping for air. Coughing frequently. Heart rate 112 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute). Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20 breaths per minute). Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg (normal below 120/80 mm Hg). SpO2 91% on room air (reference 95 to 100%). Crackles in both lung bases. Abdomen soft, not distended. No edema in either ankle. Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate left sided heart failure.

segments.text: waking at night gasping for air
segments.rationale: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Coughing frequently
segments.rationale: Cough is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Above 120/80 mm Hg, but elevated blood pressure is a cause of heart failure, not one of the pulmonary congestion or decreased cardiac output findings of left sided failure.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 beats per minute
segments.rationale: Tachycardia above 100 beats per minute is a decreased cardiac output finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: SpO2 91% on room air
segments.rationale: Below 95 to 100%. Fluid in the lungs impairs gas exchange.

segments.text: Crackles in both lung bases
segments.rationale: Crackles are a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Abdomen soft, not distended
segments.rationale: No ascites or abdominal distention, so no sign of systemic venous congestion here.

segments.text: Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees
segments.rationale: No jugular venous distention. This is an expected finding.

questions.takeaway: This client shows left sided failure: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, crackles, and low SpO2 from pulmonary congestion, plus tachycardia from decreased cardiac output. The absence of edema, ascites, and JVD argues against right sided involvement.
questions.strategy: An abnormal value is not automatically a left sided finding. For each abnormal finding, ask whether it shows blood backing into the lungs or low output, or whether it is a cause of heart failure instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Night gasping, cough, crackles, and SpO2 91% all point to fluid in the lungs.
Heart rate 112 beats per minute.

steps.action: Abnormal but not a finding of left sided failure
steps.detail: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg is a cause of heart failure.
Soft abdomen, flat neck veins.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is newly confused at 1000 after being oriented at 0700. Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg (normal below 120/80 mm Hg), heart rate 108 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20 breaths per minute), SpO2 97% on room air (reference 95 to 100%). Hands and feet are cool bilaterally. Urine output was 60 mL over the last 3 hours (reference at least 30 mL per hour). Fine crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which explanation best accounts for the confusion?

options.text: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output
options.rationale: Correct. The low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, and urine output of 20 mL per hour all show low output, and the brain is underperfused the same way the kidneys are.

options.text: Hypoxemia from fluid in the lungs
options.rationale: Crackles in the bases show some pulmonary congestion, so this is the right idea, but SpO2 97% on room air is inside 95 to 100%. The brain is getting oxygenated blood; it is not getting enough of it.

options.text: Systemic venous congestion from right sided failure
options.rationale: Systemic venous congestion produces edema, JVD, ascites, and liver findings, none of which are described. It does not explain confusion.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit from excess fluid removal
options.rationale: Low urine output and low blood pressure can fit a deficit, but crackles show the client still has fluid in the lungs, which argues against a deficit.

questions.takeaway: Confusion in heart failure can come from decreased cardiac output or from hypoxemia. Check the SpO2: when it is in range and the output findings (low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, low urine output) cluster, the cause is perfusion, not oxygenation.
questions.strategy: Hypoxemia and low output both cause confusion, and crackles make hypoxemia tempting. The deciding cue is SpO2 97% on room air.

steps.detail: Low output and hypoxemia both explain confusion.
SpO2 97% on room air is inside 95 to 100%, so hypoxemia is out.
Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg, heart rate 108, cool hands and feet, 20 mL per hour of urine: low output.
No systemic congestion findings; crackles argue against a deficit.

elimination.verdict: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with worsening heart failure. Heart rate 104 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20 breaths per minute), SpO2 92% on room air (reference 95 to 100%), 2+ edema in both ankles. Which actions belong in the nurse's ongoing assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Auscultate lung sounds and note how far up the crackles are heard
options.rationale: Lung sounds are a core heart failure assessment and show whether pulmonary congestion is spreading or clearing.

options.text: Weigh the client daily at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing
options.rationale: Daily weight with a consistent technique tracks fluid gained or lost.

options.text: Record intake and output each shift
options.rationale: Intake and output show whether fluid is being retained or removed.

options.text: Assess the apical heart rate and rhythm
options.rationale: Heart rate and rhythm are part of the nursing assessment; tachycardia is a low output finding.

options.text: Delegate auscultation of lung sounds to assistive personnel at each vital sign check
options.rationale: Assistive personnel can measure vital signs, but auscultating and interpreting lung sounds is a nursing assessment and is not delegated.

options.text: Weigh the client once a week on the same scale to limit day to day variation
options.rationale: Same scale is right, but heart failure weights are daily. A weekly weight misses a gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure assessment: respiratory status and SpO2, lung sounds, heart rate and rhythm, JVD and edema, activity tolerance, intake and output, and daily weight at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option keeps one correct detail (lung sounds, same scale) and breaks another (who assesses, how often).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Belongs, and the level of crackles matters.

steps.action: Weight, intake and output, heart rate and rhythm
steps.detail: All belong.
Auscultating and interpreting lung sounds stays with the nurse.
Heart failure weights are daily; weekly misses a 24 hour gain.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with dyspnea and 2+ edema in both ankles has a B type natriuretic peptide (BNP) of 860 pg/mL (reference below 100 pg/mL). An echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 35% (reference 55 to 70%), and the chest x ray shows an enlarged heart. Which interpretation of these results is correct?

options.text: The BNP reflects ventricular stretch, the ejection fraction shows a relaxation problem, and the film confirms the ejection fraction
options.rationale: Two errors. An ejection fraction of 35% is reduced, which is a contraction problem; a relaxation problem is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram, not the chest x ray.

options.text: The BNP reflects heart muscle damage, the ejection fraction shows a contraction problem, and the film confirms the ejection fraction
options.rationale: Two errors. Troponin is the marker of heart muscle damage, while a BNP of 860 pg/mL reflects ventricular stretch. Ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram, not the chest x ray.

options.text: The BNP reflects ventricular stretch, the ejection fraction shows a contraction problem, and the film may show congestion
options.rationale: BNP rises with ventricular stretch from fluid overload. An ejection fraction of 35% is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, a contraction problem. The chest x ray in heart failure shows cardiomegaly and congestion.

options.text: The BNP reflects heart muscle damage, the ejection fraction shows a relaxation problem, and the film may show congestion
