questions.stem: A client in the intensive care unit has had a nontunneled central line in the right internal jugular vein for 6 days. Oral temperature is 38.6 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C), heart rate is 118 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), and systolic blood pressure is 86 mm Hg (reference systolic 90 mm Hg or higher). The client has shaking chills and is newly disoriented to time. Lungs are clear, the urine is clear, and the insertion site has no redness or drainage. The infusion is running by pump at the ordered rate. Which initial treatment does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Fever, chills, low blood pressure and new disorientation with no other source in a client with a central line point to a catheter related bloodstream infection. Treatment is blood cultures twice, IV antibiotics, and catheter removal if needed.

options.text: One set of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotics are right, but blood cultures are drawn twice, not once.

options.text: A warm moist compress over the insertion site
options.rationale: This is a phlebitis intervention. The site has no redness, and the findings point to the bloodstream.

options.text: An oral antipyretic and a recheck of the temperature in 1 hour
options.rationale: An antipyretic treats the fever but not its source. Fever, chills, hypotension and new disorientation with a central line call for cultures and antibiotics, not watchful waiting.

questions.takeaway: Catheter related bloodstream infection: fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status with no other source. Draw blood cultures twice, start IV antibiotics and remove the catheter if needed.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: First rule out every other source the stem hands you: lungs, urine and site. What is left with a central line is the bloodstream infection. Then match each treatment to the complication it belongs to.

steps.detail: Clear lungs, clear urine, clean site: the line is the source.
No redness for phlebitis; an antipyretic treats the fever, not the source.
A and B share antibiotics; cultures are drawn twice, not once.

elimination.verdict: A. Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: An 87 year old client receiving hospice care in a long term care facility has had poor oral intake for 3 days. The client is alert and oriented, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg), heart rate is 96 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), and the oral mucous membranes are dry. The provider orders fluid replacement. Three peripheral IV attempts with a vein illumination device have failed. Ultrasound guided insertion is not available at the facility and would require transfer to the hospital. The hospice plan of care documents the client's wish to avoid hospital transfer. Which route does the nurse recommend to the provider?

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen at a rate of about 1 mL per minute
options.rationale: Subcutaneous infusion is used for mild to moderate dehydration in older and palliative clients and is avoided only in severe dehydration or shock. The abdomen is a common site and about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate. It needs no transfer.

options.text: Transfer to the hospital for ultrasound guided IV insertion, the standard for difficult access
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the standard for difficult access, but it requires a transfer the client has declined, and mild to moderate dehydration in a palliative client can be treated subcutaneously.

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion into the thigh at a rate of about 5 mL per minute
options.rationale: The route and site are right, but about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate for subcutaneous infusion.

options.text: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia, since it delivers all IV fluids
options.rationale: Intraosseous access does deliver all IV fluids when IV access fails, but it is for emergencies such as cardiac arrest or trauma and is limited to 24 hours. This client is alert with a blood pressure in range.

questions.takeaway: When IV access fails, match the alternative to the client's goals and urgency. Ultrasound guided insertion is the standard for difficult access. Subcutaneous infusion (hypodermoclysis) suits mild to moderate dehydration in older or palliative clients at about 1 mL per minute and is avoided in severe dehydration or shock. Intraosseous access is for emergencies and is limited to 24 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible: ultrasound guided IV insertion, the standard for difficult access, and subcutaneous infusion. The deciding cue is the documented wish to avoid hospital transfer, with findings that show neither severe dehydration nor shock.

steps.detail: Alert, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per minute: not shock, not an emergency.
Ultrasound requires a hospital transfer the client has declined.
Intraosseous access is for cardiac arrest, trauma or pediatric emergencies and lasts 24 hours at most.
Same route, but the rate limit is about 1 mL per minute, not 5.

elimination.verdict: Subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen at about 1 mL per minute.
